So "nation--people--seed children."<div eID="gen13222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">provoked--</hi>literally, "despised," namely, so as to provoke (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.30">Pr 1:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">31</reference>).<div eID="gen13223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Holy One of Israel--</hi>the peculiar heinousness of their sin, that it was against their God (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gone ... backward--</hi>literally, "estranged" (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Psa 58:3</reference>). <div eID="gen13225" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2a711e834377a26b59d74869ce0a7253d54c756: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8311"/><div sID="gen13226" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8311"/><hi type="bold">5. Why--</hi>rather, as Vulgate, "On what part." Image from a body covered all over with marks of blows (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>). There is no part in which you have not been smitten.<div eID="gen13226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head ... sick, &c.--</hi>not referring, as it is commonly quoted, to their sins, but to the universality of their punishment. However, sin, the moral disease of the head or intellect, and the heart, is doubtless made its own punishment (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">Ho 8:11</reference>). "Sick," literally, "is in a state of sickness" [Gesenius]; "has passed into sickness" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13227" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c3ca80505e818c327ff9b226c709608e891597f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8312"/><div sID="gen13228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8312"/>6. From the lowest to the highest of the people; "the ancient and honorable, the head, the prophet that teacheth lies, the tail." See <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13-Isa.9.16">Is 9:13-16</reference>. He first states their wretched condition, obvious to all (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6-Isa.1.9">Is 1:6-9</reference>); and then, not previously, their irreligious state, the cause of it.<div eID="gen13228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wounds--</hi>judicially inflicted (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen13229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mollified with ointment--</hi>The art of medicine in the East consists chiefly in external applications (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.34">Lu 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.14">Jas 5:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13230" type="x-p"/>
entries.93f7b9426be6bbaf1df202f9edd0c11f5886ebac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8313"/><div sID="gen13231" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8313"/>7. Judah had not in Uzziah's reign recovered from the ravages of the Syrians in Joash's reign (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.24">2Ch 24:24</reference>), and of Israel in Amaziah's reign (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.13">2Ch 25:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.23">23</reference>, &c.). Compare Isaiah's contemporary (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.6-Amos.4.11">Am 4:6-11</reference>), where, as here (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Is 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>), Israel is compared to "Sodom and Gomorrah," because of the judgments on it by "fire."<div eID="gen13231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in your presence--</hi>before your eyes: without your being able to prevent them.<div eID="gen13232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desolate, &c.--</hi>literally, "there is desolation, such as one might look for from foreign" invaders. <div eID="gen13233" type="x-p"/>
entries.61a83a2ba301c304e0a1893e1cbe4c7d19b5301d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8314"/><div sID="gen13234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8314"/><hi type="bold">8. daughter of Zion--</hi>the city (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">Psa 9:14</reference>), Jerusalem and its inhabitants (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">2Ki 19:21</reference>): "daughter" (feminine, singular being used as a neuter collective noun), equivalent to sons (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.6">Is 12:6</reference>, Margin) [Maurer]. Metropolis or "mother-city" is the corresponding term. The idea of youthful beauty is included in "daughter."<div eID="gen13234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left--</hi>as a remnant escaping the general destruction.<div eID="gen13235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cottage--</hi>a hut, made to give temporary shelter to the caretaker of the vineyard.<div eID="gen13236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lodge--</hi>not permanent.<div eID="gen13237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">besieged--</hi>rather, as "left," and <reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Is 1:9</reference> require, preserved, namely, from the desolation all round [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13238" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ec060ca2e6da1930be8d8ccbe7c25ce082a412d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8315"/><div sID="gen13239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8315"/>9. Jehovah of Sabaoth, that is, God of the angelic and starry hosts (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.5">Psa 59:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.4">147:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.148.2">148:2</reference>). The latter were objects of idolatry, called hence Sabaism (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.16">2Ki 17:16</reference>). God is above even them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.26">1Ch 16:26</reference>). "The groves" were symbols of these starry hosts; it was their worship of Sabaoth instead of the Lord of Sabaoth, which had caused the present desolation (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.18">2Ch 24:18</reference>). It needed no less a power than His, to preserve even a "remnant." Condescending grace for the elect's sake, since He has no need of us, seeing that He has countless hosts to serve Him. <div eID="gen13239" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c31d0a3d0b43683d2089977a634b03f1abe8a6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8316"/><div sID="gen13240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8316"/><hi type="bold">10. Sodom--</hi>spiritually (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.24">Ge 19:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">Jr 23:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.46">Eze 16:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>). <div eID="gen13240" type="x-p"/>
entries.9cf5f069e225178aeda6ff693544c5d521924589: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8317"/><div sID="gen13241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8317"/>11. God does not here absolutely disparage sacrifice, which is as old and universal as sin (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.21">Ge 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">4:4</reference>), and sin is almost as old as the world; but sacrifice, unaccompanied with obedience of heart and life (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>; Psa 50:9-13; 51:16-19; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>). Positive precepts are only means; moral obedience is the end. A foreshadowing of the gospel, when the One real sacrifice was to supersede all the shadowy ones, and "bring in everlasting righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Da 9:24-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.14">He 10:1-14</reference>).<div eID="gen13241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full--</hi>to satiety; weary of<div eID="gen13242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burnt offerings--</hi>burnt whole, except the blood, which was sprinkled about the altar.<div eID="gen13243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fat--</hi>not to be eaten by man, but burnt on the altar (<reference osisRef="Lev.3.4">Le 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.11">5, 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen13244" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7ac01cb279ffee8dc59401876b006ba602020c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8318"/><div sID="gen13245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8318"/><hi type="bold">12. appear before me--</hi>in the temple where the Shekinah, resting on the ark, was the symbol of God's presence (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">Ex 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.2">Psa 42:2</reference>).<div eID="gen13245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who hath required this--</hi>as if you were doing God a service by such hypocritical offerings (<reference osisRef="Job.35.7">Job 35:7</reference>). God did require it (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Ex 23:17</reference>), but not in this spirit (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.6">Mi 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen13246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">courts--</hi>areas, in which the worshippers were. None but priests entered the temple itself. <div eID="gen13247" type="x-p"/>
entries.2bd8c7e8063bd63848472777d90ef39b515b7604: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8319"/><div sID="gen13248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8319"/><hi type="bold">13. oblations--</hi>unbloody; "meat (old English sense, not flesh) offerings," that is, of flour, fruits, oil, &c. (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.1-Lev.2.13">Le 2:1-13</reference>). Hebrew, mincha.<div eID="gen13248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">incense--</hi>put upon the sacrifices, and burnt on the altar of incense. Type of prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Re 8:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new moons--</hi>observed as festivals (<reference osisRef="Num.10.10">Nu 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.28.11">28:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.28.14">14</reference>) with sacrifices and blowing of silver trumpets.<div eID="gen13250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sabbaths--</hi>both the seventh day and the beginning and closing days of the great feasts (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.24-Lev.23.39">Le 23:24-39</reference>).<div eID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">away with--</hi>bear, Maurer translates, "I cannot bear iniquity and the solemn meeting," that is, the meeting associated with iniquity--literally, the closing days of the feasts; so the great days (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Le 23:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>). <div eID="gen13252" type="x-p"/>
entries.b67a2d836b08c5cb9c7b0481b83b72b81ac5e24c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8320"/><div sID="gen13253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8320"/><hi type="bold">14. appointed--</hi>the sabbath, passover, pentecost, day of atonement, and feast of tabernacles [Hengstenberg]; they alone were fixed to certain times of the year.<div eID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weary--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.24">Is 43:24</reference>). <div eID="gen13254" type="x-p"/>
entries.58ee6da1e93b1a844afbdb5761985db725dee2de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8321"/><div sID="gen13255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8321"/>15. (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Pr 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.43">La 3:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">44</reference>).<div eID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread ... hands--</hi>in prayer (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.22">1Ki 8:22</reference>). Hebrew, "bloods," for all heinous sins, persecution of God's servants especially (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Mt 23:35</reference>). It was the vocation of the prophets to dispel the delusion, so contrary to the law itself (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.16">De 10:16</reference>), that outward ritualism would satisfy God. <div eID="gen13256" type="x-p"/>
entries.76f2d6d0be6e62adca718a041ca1a312beac8f5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8322"/><div sID="gen13257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8322"/>16. God saith to the sinner, "Wash you," &c., that he, finding his inability to "make" himself "clean," may cry to God, Wash me, cleanse me (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.2">Psa 51:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">7, 10</reference>).<div eID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before mine eyes--</hi>not mere outward reformation before man's eyes, who cannot, as God, see into the heart (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">Jr 32:19</reference>). <div eID="gen13258" type="x-p"/>
entries.82b2ad83ca8ef43869e4eacd4f67c22e698a2c64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8323"/><div sID="gen13259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8323"/><hi type="bold">17. seek judgment--</hi>justice, as magistrates, instead of seeking bribes (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge--</hi>vindicate (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Psa 68:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jas 1:27</reference>). <div eID="gen13260" type="x-p"/>
entries.a75166d611fb19dc4ced4c9b8485de116a2ce005: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8324"/><div sID="gen13261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8324"/>18. God deigns to argue the case with us, that all may see the just, nay, loving principle of His dealings with men (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Is 43:26</reference>).<div eID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scarlet--</hi>the color of Jesus Christ's robe when bearing our "sins" (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.28">Mt 27:28</reference>). So Rahab's thread (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.18">Jos 2:18</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Lev.14.4">Le 14:4</reference>). The rabbins say that when the lot used to be taken, a scarlet fillet was bound on the scapegoat's head, and after the high priest had confessed his and the people's sins over it, the fillet became white: the miracle ceased, according to them, forty years before the destruction of Jerusalem, that is, exactly when Jesus Christ was crucified; a remarkable admission of adversaries. Hebrew for "scarlet" radically means double-dyed; so the deep-fixed permanency of sin in the heart, which no mere tears can wash away.<div eID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">snow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.51.7">Psa 51:7</reference>). Repentance is presupposed, before sin can be made white as snow (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.19">Is 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>); it too is God's gift (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>, Lam 5:21, Acts 5:31).<div eID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">red--</hi>refers to "blood" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as wool--</hi>restored to its original undyed whiteness. This verse shows that the old fathers did not look only for transitory promises (Article VII, Book of Common Prayer). For sins of ignorance, and such like, alone had trespass offerings appointed for them; greater guilt therefore needed a greater sacrifice, for, "without shedding of blood there was no remission"; but none such was appointed, and yet forgiveness was promised and expected; therefore spiritual Jews must have looked for the One Mediator of both Old Testament and New Testament, though dimly understood. <div eID="gen13265" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd236885a758fd872d8a7efa8434c7faf18c85fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8325"/><div sID="gen13266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8325"/>19-20. Temporal blessings in "the land of their possession" were prominent in the Old Testament promises, as suited to the childhood of the Church (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.17">Ex 3:17</reference>). New Testament spiritual promises derive their imagery from the former (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mt 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen13266" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa44833fb28e9e5b2b0b1a9b6c20ae9c60d1d5d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8327"/><div sID="gen13268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8327"/><hi type="bold">21. faithful--</hi>as a wife (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Ho 2:19</reference>, 20).<div eID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">harlot--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.28-Ezek.16.35">Eze 16:28-35</reference>).<div eID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness lodged--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">murderers--</hi>murderous oppressors, as the antithesis requires (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.15">1Jo 3:15</reference>). <div eID="gen13271" type="x-p"/>
entries.316418ab2f3587b38596219b672223bc99f57bef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8328"/><div sID="gen13272" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8328"/>22. Thy princes and people are degenerate in "solid worth," equivalent to "silver" (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.28">Jr 6:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.18">Eze 22:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.19">19</reference>), and in their use of the living Word, equivalent to "wine" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.9">So 7:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mixed--</hi>literally, "circumcised." So the Arabic, "to murder" wine, equivalent to dilute it. <div eID="gen13273" type="x-p"/>
entries.a77b65d5a624b3fa03417e63441a8289feb8f0e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8329"/><div sID="gen13274" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8329"/><hi type="bold">23. companions of thieves--</hi>by connivance (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.24">Pr 29:24</reference>).<div eID="gen13274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gifts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:12</reference>). A nation's corruption begins with its rulers. <div eID="gen13275" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3b64d94ff03851b40322a622320d0393c8ab072: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8330"/><div sID="gen13276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8330"/><hi type="bold">24. Lord ... Lord--</hi>Adonai, Jehovah.<div eID="gen13276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty One of Israel--</hi>mighty to take vengeance, as before, to save.<div eID="gen13277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ah--</hi>indignation.<div eID="gen13278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ease me--</hi>My long tried patience will find relief in at last punishing the guilty (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Eze 5:13</reference>). God's language condescends to human conceptions. <div eID="gen13279" type="x-p"/>
entries.c298e037681b278d09cdb141094a917c5f5f898b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8331"/><div sID="gen13280" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8331"/><hi type="bold">25. turn ... hand--</hi>not in wrath, but in grace (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zec 13:7</reference>), "upon thee," as <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Is 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">27</reference> show; contrasted with the enemies, of whom He will avenge Himself (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Is 1:24</reference>).<div eID="gen13280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purely--</hi>literally, "as alkali purifies."<div eID="gen13281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy dross--</hi>not thy sins, but the sinful persons (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.29">Jr 6:29</reference>); "enemies" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Is 1:24</reference>); degenerate princes (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Is 1:22</reference>), intermingled with the elect "remnant" of grace.<div eID="gen13282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tin--</hi>Hebrew, bedil, here the alloy of lead, tin, &c., separated by smelting from the silver. The pious Bishop Bedell took his motto from this. <div eID="gen13283" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c9f01ff365146ff64d43a680f0d5ea4e02b9b92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8332"/><div sID="gen13284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8332"/>26. As the degeneracy had shown itself most in the magistrates (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.17-Isa.1.23">Is 1:17-23</reference>), so, at the "restoration," these shall be such as the theocracy "at the first" had contemplated, namely, after the Babylonish restoration in part and typically, but fully and antitypically under Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Is 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">52:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.7">Jr 33:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>).<div eID="gen13284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithful--</hi>no longer "an harlot." <div eID="gen13285" type="x-p"/>
entries.e07871fff50d59dbcb8670ffb8ddbbe1418502af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8333"/><div sID="gen13286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8333"/><hi type="bold">27. redeemed--</hi>temporarily, civilly, and morally; type of the spiritual redemption by the price of Jesus Christ's blood (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>), the foundation of "judgment" and "righteousness," and so of pardon. The judgment and righteousness are God's first (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">Ro 3:26</reference>); so they become man's when "converted" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Ro 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">4</reference>); typified in the display of God's "justice," then exhibited in delivering His covenant-people, whereby justice or "righteousness" was produced in them.<div eID="gen13286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">converts--</hi>so Maurer. But Margin, "they that return of her," namely the remnant that return from captivity. However, as Isaiah had not yet expressly foretold the Babylonian captivity, the English Version is better. <div eID="gen13287" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e5e6fab3a119c2ef8786aab52a84038bb4818e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8334"/><div sID="gen13288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8334"/><hi type="bold">28. destruction--</hi>literally, "breaking into shivers" (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>). The prophets hasten forward to the final extinction of the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.15">20:15</reference>); of which antecedent judgments are types. <div eID="gen13288" type="x-p"/>
entries.7859b20c7c5441aecb7ba040d8a6258c04cb8abb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8335"/><div sID="gen13289" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8335"/><hi type="bold">29. ashamed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Ro 6:21</reference>).<div eID="gen13289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oaks--</hi>Others translate the "terebinth" or "turpentine tree." Groves were dedicated to idols. Our Druids took their name from the Greek for "oaks." A sacred tree is often found in Assyrian sculpture; symbol of the starry hosts, Saba.<div eID="gen13290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gardens--</hi>planted enclosures for idolatry; the counterpart of the garden of Eden. <div eID="gen13291" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b33d0f0b4a854f8149727c987fde1274ca106b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8336"/><div sID="gen13292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8336"/><hi type="bold">30. oak--</hi>Ye shall be like the "oaks," the object of your "desire" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>). People become like the gods they worship; they never rise above their level (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.18">Psa 135:18</reference>). So men's sins become their own scourges (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.9">Jr 2:9</reference>). The leaf of the idol oak fades by a law of necessary consequence, having no living sap or "water" from God. So "garden" answers to "gardens" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen13292" type="x-p"/>
entries.70da0a03e641ebb3d1f5d645beba7148b828bfb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8337"/><div sID="gen13293" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8337"/><hi type="bold">31. strong--</hi>powerful rulers (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maker of it--</hi>rather, his work. He shall be at once the fuel, "tow," and the cause of the fire, by kindling the first "spark."<div eID="gen13294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">both--</hi>the wicked ruler, and "his work," which "is as a spark." <chapter eID="Isa.1"/>

entries.960e4862dec6a822055555c40b579d0ccd5216ff: <div eID="gen26171" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of the Prophet Isaiah</title> <div sID="gen26172" type="x-p"/> On the term prophet, and on the nature and several kinds of prophecy, I have already discoursed in different parts of this work. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference> (note), and the preface to the four Gospels, and Acts of the Apostles. A few things only require to be recapitulated. נבא naba signifies not only to foretell future events, but also to pray and supplicate; and נביא nabi, the prophet, was by office not only a declarer of events still future, but the general preacher of the day; and as he frequently foresaw the approach of disastrous times, such was the wickedness of the people, he employed his time in counseling sinners to turn from the error of their ways, and in making strong prayer and supplication to God to avert the threatened judgments: for such predictions, however apparently positive in their terms, were generally conditional; strange as this may appear to some who, through their general ignorance of every thing but the peculiarities of their own creed, suppose that every occurrence is impelled by an irresistible necessity. <div eID="gen26172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26173" type="x-p"/> To his own conduct, in reference to such matters, God has been pleased to give us a key (see Jeremiah 18.) which opens all difficulties, and furnishes us with a general comment on his own providence. God is absolute master of his own ways; and as he has made man a free agent, whatever concerns him in reference to futurity, on which God is pleased to express his mind in the way of prophecy, there is a condition generally implied or expressed. As this is but seldom attended to by partial interpreters, who wish by their doctrine of fatalism to bind even God himself, many contradictory sentiments are put in the mouths of his prophets. <div eID="gen26173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26174" type="x-p"/> In ancient times those who were afterwards called Prophets were termed Seers; <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9">1Sam 9:9</reference>. הראה haroeh, the seeing person; he who perceives mentally what the design of God is. Sometimes called also חזה chozeh, the man who has visions, or supernatural revelations; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">1Kgs 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13">2Kgs 17:13</reference>. Both these terms are translated seer in our common Version. They were sometimes called men of God, and messengers or angels of God. In their case it was ever understood that all God's prophets had an extraordinary commission and had their message given them by immediate inspiration. <div eID="gen26174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26175" type="x-p"/> In this the heathen copied after the people of God. They also had their prophets and seers; and hence their augurs and auguries, their haruspices, and priestesses, and their oracles; all pretending to be divinely inspired, and to declare nothing but the truth; for what was truth and fact among the former, was affected and pretended among the latter. <div eID="gen26175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26176" type="x-p"/> Many prophets and seers are mentioned in the sacred writings; but, fragments and insulated prophecies excepted, we have the works of only Sixteen; four of whom are termed the former or larger prophets, and twelve, the latter or minor prophets. They have these epithets, not from priority of time, or from minor importance, but merely from the places they occupy in the present arrangement of the books in the Bible, and from the relative size of their productions. <div eID="gen26176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26177" type="x-p"/> The Jews reckon forty-eight prophets, and seven prophetesses; and Epiphanius, in a fragment preserved by Cotelerius, reckons not fewer than seventy-three prophets, and ten prophetesses; but in both collections there are many which have no Scriptural pretensions to such a distinguished rank. <div eID="gen26177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26178" type="x-p"/> The succession of prophets in the Jewish Church is well worthy of note, because it not only manifests the merciful regards of God towards that people, but also the uninterrupted succession of the prophetic influence, at least from Moses to Malachi, if not before; for this gift was not withheld under the patriarchal dispensation; indeed we might boldly ask any man to show when the time was in which God left himself without a witness of this kind. <div eID="gen26178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26179" type="x-p"/> To show this succession, I shall endeavor to give the different prophets in order of time. <div eID="gen26179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26180" type="x-p"/> 1. The first man, Adam, has an undoubted right to stand at the head of the prophets, as he does at the head of the human race. His declaration concerning marriage, "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and cleave to his wife," is so truly prophetic, that no doubt can be formed on the subject. There was then nothing in nature or experience to justify such an assertion; and he could have it only by Divine inspiration. The millions of instances which have since occurred, and the numerous laws which have been founded on this principle among all the nations of the earth, show with what precision the declaration was conceived, and with what truth it was published to the world. Add to this, his correct knowledge of the nature of the different animals, so that he could impose on them names expressive of their respective natures or propensities; which proves that he must have acted under a Divine inspiration; for known only to God are all his works from the beginning. <div eID="gen26180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26181" type="x-p"/> 2. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is expressly called a prophet; and St. Jude, <reference osisRef="Jde.1.14">Jde 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jde.1.15">Jde 1:15</reference>, has preserved a fragment of one of his prophecies, relative to the corruption of the ante-diluvian world, and the approaching judgments of God. <div eID="gen26181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26182" type="x-p"/> 3. Noah was a prophet and preacher of righteousness, and predicted the general deluge, and the time of respite which God in his mercy had granted to the offenders of that age. <div eID="gen26182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26183" type="x-p"/> 4. Abraham is expressly called a prophet also, <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>; and it appears from <reference osisRef="Psa.105.15">Psa 105:15</reference>, that he partook of the Divine anointing. <div eID="gen26183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26184" type="x-p"/> 5. Isaac, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.27">Gen 27:27</reference>, predicted the future greatness of his son Jacob, and of the race that was to spring from him. <div eID="gen26184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26185" type="x-p"/> 6. Jacob was so especially favored with the prophetic gift, that he distinctly foretold what should happen to each of his sons. See Genesis 49. <div eID="gen26185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26186" type="x-p"/> 7. Joseph was favored with several prophetic visions, and had the gift of interpreting dreams which portended future occurrences; (see Genesis 27, 40, 41.); and foretold the redemption of the Israelites from Egypt; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Gen 50:25</reference>. Thus far the prophetic influence extended through the patriarchal dispensation for about two thousand three hundred and seventy years from the creation. <div eID="gen26186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26187" type="x-p"/> With the Jewish dispensation the prophetic gift revived; and, <div eID="gen26187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26188" type="x-p"/> 8. Moses became one of the most eminent prophets that had ever appeared. He not only enjoyed the continual prophetic afflatus, but had such visions of and intercourse with God as no other person either before or since was favored with; and by which he was highly qualified to perform the arduous work which God had given him to do, and to frame that Code of Laws which had no equal before the promulgation of the Gospel. See <reference osisRef="Deu.24.10">Deu 24:10</reference>. He predicted expressly the coming of the Messiah. See <reference osisRef="Deu.18.18">Deu 18:18</reference>. <div eID="gen26188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26189" type="x-p"/> 9. Aaron, the brother of Moses, his prime minister and God's high priest, was also a partaker of his Divine influence, and declared the will of God to Pharaoh and the Israelites, not merely from information received from Moses, but also by immediate communication from God. See <reference osisRef="Exo.4.15">Exo 4:15</reference>. <div eID="gen26189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26190" type="x-p"/> 10. Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, is expressly called a prophetess, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.2">Num 12:2</reference>. <div eID="gen26190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26191" type="x-p"/> 11. Joshua, who succeeded Moses, was a partaker of the same grace. He was appointed by Moses under the especial direction of God; <reference osisRef="Num.27.18-Num.27.23">Num 27:18-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.34.9">Deu 34:9</reference>; and has always been reckoned among the Jews as one of the prophets. See Sirach 46:1-6. Though I cannot place them in the same rank, yet it is necessary to state that, by the Jews, several of the judges are classed among the prophets; such as Othniel, Ehud, Samson, and Barak. <div eID="gen26191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26192" type="x-p"/> 12. Deborah, the coadjutor of Barak, is called a prophetess, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.4">Jdg 4:4</reference>. During her time, and down to the days of Eli the high priest, prophecy had been very scarce, there having been very few on whom the Spirit of the Lord had rested; for "the word of the Lord was scarce in those days, and there was no open vision;" <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1Sam 3:1</reference>. <div eID="gen26192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26193" type="x-p"/> 13. Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, is supposed to have partaken of the spirit of prophecy; and to have foretold, at least indirectly, the advent of the Messiah, and the glory that should be revealed under the Gospel. See her Song, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.10">1Sam 2:1-10</reference>. And what renders this more likely is, that it is on the model, and with many of the expressions, of this song, that the blessed Virgin composed her Magnificat, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.46-Luk.1.55">Luk 1:46-55</reference>. <div eID="gen26193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26194" type="x-p"/> 14. Samuel, her son, was one of the most eminent of the Jewish prophets, and was the last, and indeed the greatest, of the judges of Israel. In his time the prophetic influence seems to have rested upon many; so that we find even whole schools or colleges of prophets which were under his direction. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sam 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.10">1Sam 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.20">1Sam 19:20</reference>, and elsewhere. <div eID="gen26194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26195" type="x-p"/> 15. David united in himself the character of prophet and king, in the most eminent manner; and from his reign down to the captivity the succession was not only not interrupted, but these extraordinary messengers of God became very numerous. <div eID="gen26195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26196" type="x-p"/> 16. Gad flourished under his reign, and was emphatically called David's Seer, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.11">2Sam 24:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.9">1Chr 21:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.19">1Chr 21:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.20">1Chr 21:20</reference>; and it appears that he had written a Book of Prophecies, which is now lost, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">1Chr 29:29</reference>. <div eID="gen26196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26197" type="x-p"/> 17. Nathan lived also under the same reign, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sam 7:2</reference>; and, in conjunction with Gad, composed a book of the acts of David, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">1Chr 29:29</reference>. <div eID="gen26197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26198" type="x-p"/> 18. To Solomon also, son of David, the prophetic gift has been attributed. This might be implied in the extraordinary wisdom with which God had endowed him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.5-1Kgs.3.9">1Kgs 3:5-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.7">2Chr 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.12">2Chr 7:12</reference>; and in his writings several prophetic declarations may be found, even independently of the supposed reference to Christ and his Church in the Song of Solomon. <div eID="gen26198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26199" type="x-p"/> 19. Iddo is termed a Seer, <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.15">2Chr 12:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.22">2Chr 13:22</reference>; and was one of Solomon's biographers. <div eID="gen26199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26200" type="x-p"/> 20. Shemaiah lived under Rehoboam; he is called a man of God, and to him the word of prophecy came relative to Judah and Benjamin, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.22-1Kgs.12.24">1Kgs 12:22-24</reference>. Some think this was the same person who was sent to Jeroboam relative to his idolatry; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.1">1Kgs 13:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen26200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26201" type="x-p"/> 21. Ahijah, the Shilonite, prophesied to Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.29-1Kgs.11.39">1Kgs 11:29-39</reference>. <div eID="gen26201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26202" type="x-p"/> 22. Hanani the Seer prophesied under Azariah and Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Chr 16:7</reference>. <div eID="gen26202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26203" type="x-p"/> 23. Jehu, son of Hanani, prophesied under Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.1">1Kgs 16:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.7">1Kgs 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Chr 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.2">2Chr 19:2</reference>; and <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.34">2Chr 20:34</reference>. <div eID="gen26203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26204" type="x-p"/> 24. Azariah, the son of Oded, prophesied under Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1">2Chr 15:1</reference>. <div eID="gen26204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26205" type="x-p"/> 25. Elijah prophesied under the reign of Ahab and Jezebel. <div eID="gen26205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26206" type="x-p"/> 26. Elisha succeeded Elijah under the same reigns. And these eminent men had many disciples on whom the spirit of prophecy rested. They, and their masters, Elijah and Elisha, prophesied in the kingdoms both of Israel and Judah. Their histories make a prominent part of the first and second Books of Kings; and are well known. <div eID="gen26206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26207" type="x-p"/> 27. Micaiah, the son of Imlah, prophesied under the same reign, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.9">1Kgs 21:9</reference>. <div eID="gen26207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26208" type="x-p"/> 28. Hosea prophesied under Jeroboam the second, king of Israel, and under the reign of Uzziah, king of Judah. <div eID="gen26208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26209" type="x-p"/> 29. Isaiah was contemporary with Hosea, but probably began to prophesy a little later than he did. <div eID="gen26209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26210" type="x-p"/> 30. Amos prophesied about the same time. <div eID="gen26210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26211" type="x-p"/> 31. Jonah, son of Amittai, is supposed to have been contemporary with the above. <div eID="gen26211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26212" type="x-p"/> 32. Eliezer, the son of Dodavah, prophesied against Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.37">2Chr 20:37</reference>. <div eID="gen26212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26213" type="x-p"/> 33. Jahaziel, son of Zechariah, prophesied against Judah and Israel under the same reign, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14">2Chr 20:14</reference>. <div eID="gen26213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26214" type="x-p"/> 34. Micah prophesied against Samaria and Jerusalem, in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. <div eID="gen26214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26215" type="x-p"/> 35. Oded, father of Azariah, prophesied against Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Chr 15:8</reference>. <div eID="gen26215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26216" type="x-p"/> 36. Nahum prophesied under Hezekiah. <div eID="gen26216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26217" type="x-p"/> 37. Joel, under Josiah. <div eID="gen26217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26218" type="x-p"/> 38. Jeremiah, about the same time. <div eID="gen26218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26219" type="x-p"/> 39. Zephaniah, under the same reign. See their prophecies. <div eID="gen26219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26220" type="x-p"/> 40. Huldah, the prophetess, was contemporary with the above. <div eID="gen26220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26221" type="x-p"/> 41. Igdaliah, called a man of God, and probably a prophet, was contemporary with Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.4">Jer 35:4</reference>. <div eID="gen26221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26222" type="x-p"/> 42. Habakkuk lived about the end of the reign of Josiah, or the beginning of that of Jehoiakim. <div eID="gen26222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26223" type="x-p"/> 43. Ezekiel lived under the captivity; and prophesied in Mesopotamia, about the time that Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen26223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26224" type="x-p"/> 44. Obadiah lived in Judea, after the capture of Jerusalem and before the desolation of Idumea by Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen26224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26225" type="x-p"/> 45. Daniel prophesied in Babylon during the captivity. <div eID="gen26225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26226" type="x-p"/> 46. Haggai prophesied during and after the captivity. <div eID="gen26226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26227" type="x-p"/> 47. Urijah, the son of Shemaiah, prophesied under Jehoiakim. See <reference osisRef="Jer.26.20">Jer 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.21">Jer 26:21</reference>. <div eID="gen26227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26228" type="x-p"/> 48. Zechariah, son of Barachiah, flourished in the second year of Darius, a
entries.68b7b9b94d859f78d6f9f5c6bb800ae251b4e1e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26322" type="x-p"/> Hear, O heavens "Hear, O ye heavens" - God is introduced as entering into a public action, or pleading, before the whole world, against his disobedient people. The prophet, as herald or officer to proclaim the summons to the court, calls upon all created beings, celestial and terrestrial, to attend and bear witness to the truth of his plea and the justice of his cause. The same scene is more fully displayed in the noble exordium of <reference osisRef="Psa.1.1-Psa.1.6">Psa 1:1-6</reference>, where God summons all mankind, from east to west, to be present to hear his appeal; and the solemnity is held on Sion, where he is attended with the same terrible pomp that accompanied him on Mount Sinai: - "A consuming fire goes before him <div eID="gen26322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26323" type="x-p"/> And round him rages a violent tempest: <div eID="gen26323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26324" type="x-p"/> He calleth the heavens from above. <div eID="gen26324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26325" type="x-p"/> And the earth, that he may contend in judgment with his people." <reference osisRef="Psa.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.50.4">Psa 50:4</reference>. <div eID="gen26325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26326" type="x-p"/> By the same bold figure, Micah calls upon the mountains, that is, the whole country of Judea, to attend to him, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Isa 6:2</reference> : - "Arise, plead thou before the mountains, <div eID="gen26326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26327" type="x-p"/> And let the hills hear thy voice. <div eID="gen26327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26328" type="x-p"/> Hear, O ye mountains, the controversy of Jehovah; <div eID="gen26328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26329" type="x-p"/> And ye, O ye strong foundations of the earth: <div eID="gen26329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26330" type="x-p"/> For Jehovah hath a controversy with his people, <div eID="gen26330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26331" type="x-p"/> And he will plead his cause against Israel." <div eID="gen26331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26332" type="x-p"/> With the like invocation, Moses introduces his sublime song, the design of which was the same as that of this prophecy, "to testify as a witness, against the Israelites," for their disobedience, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference> : - "Give ear, O ye heavens, and I will speak; <div eID="gen26332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26333" type="x-p"/> And let the earth hear the words of my mouth." <reference osisRef="Deu.32.1">Deu 32:1</reference>. <div eID="gen26333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26334" type="x-p"/> This, in the simple yet strong oratorical style of Moses, is, "I call heaven and earth to witness against thee this day; life and death have I set before thee; the blessing and the curse: choose now life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed." <reference osisRef="Deu.30.19">Deu 30:19</reference>. The poetical style, by an apostrophe, sets the personification in a much stronger light. <div eID="gen26334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26335" type="x-p"/> Hath spoken "That speaketh" - I render it in the present time, pointing it דבר dober. There seems to be an impropriety in demanding attention to a speech already delivered. But the present reading may stand, as the prophet may be here understood to declare to the people what the Lord had first spoken to him. <div eID="gen26335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26336" type="x-p"/> I have nourished - The Septuagint have εγεννησα, "I have begotten." Instead of גדלתי giddalti, they read ילדתי yaladti; the word little differing from the other, and perhaps more proper; which the Chaldee likewise seems to favor; "vocavi eos filios." See <reference osisRef="Exo.4.22">Exo 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.9">Jer 31:9</reference>.
entries.f65151ad9c07554038a2e36a48568494eb31df08: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26337" type="x-p"/> The ox knoweth - An amplification of the gross insensibility of the disobedient Jews, by comparing them with the most heavy and stupid of all animals, yet not so insensible as they. Bochart has well illustrated the comparison, and shown the peculiar force of it. "He sets them lower than the beasts, and even than the most stupid of all beasts, for there is scarcely any more so than the ox and the ass. Yet these acknowledge their master; they know the manger of their lord; by whom they are fed, not for their own, but for his good; neither are they looked upon as children, but as beasts of burden; neither are they advanced to honors, but oppressed with great and daily labors. While the Israelites, chosen by the mere favor of God, adopted as sons, promoted to the highest dignity, yet acknowledged not their Lord and their God; but despised his commandments, though in the highest degree equitable and just." Hieroz. i., Colossians 409. <div eID="gen26337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26338" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah's comparison to the same purpose is equally elegant, but has not so much spirit and severity as this of Isaiah. "Even the stork in the heavens knoweth her season; <div eID="gen26338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26339" type="x-p"/> And the turtle, and the swallow, and the crane, observe the time of their coming: <div eID="gen26339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26340" type="x-p"/> But my people doth not know the judgment of Jehovah. <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer 8:7</reference>. <div eID="gen26340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26341" type="x-p"/> Hosea has given a very elegant turn to the same image, in the way of metaphor or allegory: - "I drew them with human cords, with the bands of love: <div eID="gen26341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26342" type="x-p"/> And I was to them as he that lifteth up the yoke upon their cheek; <div eID="gen26342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26343" type="x-p"/> And I laid down their fodder before them." <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos 11:4</reference>. <div eID="gen26343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26344" type="x-p"/> Salomo ben Melech thus explains the middle part of the verse, which is somewhat obscure: "I was to them at their desire as they that have compassion on a heifer, lest she be overworked in ploughing; and that lift up the yoke from off her neck, and rest it upon her cheek that she may not still draw, but rest from her labor an hour or two in the day." <div eID="gen26344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26345" type="x-p"/> But Israel - The Septuagint, Syriac, Aquila, Theodotion, and Vulgate, read וישראל veyisrael, But Israel, adding the conjunction, which being rendered as an adversative, sets the opposition in a stronger light. <div eID="gen26345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26346" type="x-p"/> Doth not know - The same ancient versions agree in adding Me, which very properly answers, and indeed is almost necessarily required to answer, the words possessor and lord preceding. Ισραηλ δε ΜΕ ουκ εγνω; Sept. "Israel autem me non cognovit," Vulg. Ισραηλ δε ΜΟΥ ουκ εγνω; Aquil., Theod. The testimony of so scrupulous an interpreter as Aquila is of great weight in this case. And both his and Theodotion's rendering is such as shows plainly that they did not add the word ΜΟΥ to help out the sense, for it only embarrasses it. It also clearly determines what was the original reading in the old copies from which they translated. It could not be ידעני yedani, which most obviously answers to the version of the Septuagint and Vulgate, for it does not accord with that of Aquila and Theodotion. The version of these latter interpreters, however injudicious, clearly ascertains both the phrase, and the order of the words of the original Hebrew; it was ישראל אותי לא ידע veyisrael othi lo yada. The word אותי othi has been lost out of the text. The very same phrase is used by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.22">Jer 4:22</reference>, עמי אותי לא ידעו ammi othi lo yadau. And the order of the words must have been as above represented; for they have joined ישראל yisrael, with אותי othi, as in regimine; they could not have taken it in this sense, Israel meus non cognovit, had either this phrase or the order of the words been different. I have endeavored to set this matter in a clear light, as it is the first example of a whole word lost out of the text, of which the reader will find many other plain examples in the course of these notes. But Rosenmuller contends that this is unnecessary, as the passage may be translated, "Israel knows nothing: my people have no understanding." The Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate, read ועמי veammi, "and my people;" and so likewise sixteen MSS. of Kennicott, and fourteen of De Rossi.
entries.2dbcc6f744bd637c46902ce34a421816213b8526: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26347" type="x-p"/> Ah sinful nation "Degenerate" - Five MSS., one of them ancient, read משחתים moschathim, without the first י yod, in hophal corrupted, not corrupters. See the same word in the same form, and in the same sense, <reference osisRef="Pro.25.26">Pro 25:26</reference>. <div eID="gen26347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26348" type="x-p"/> Are corrupters "Are estranged" - Thirty-two MSS., five ancient, and two editions, read נזורו nazoru; which reading determines the word to be from the root זור zur, to alienate, not from נזר nazar, to separate; so Kimchi understands it. See also Annotat. in Noldium, 68. <div eID="gen26348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26349" type="x-p"/> They are gone away backward "They have turned their backs upon him" - So Kimchi explains it:" they have turned unto him the back and not the face." See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jer 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.24">Jer 7:24</reference>. I have been forced to render this line paraphrastically; as the verbal translation, "they are estranged backward," would have been unintelligible.
entries.7282f1dc10b573a89b0f51dd9666fe5f5e799c58: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26350" type="x-p"/> Why should ye be stricken any more "On what part," etc.? - The Vulgate renders על מה al meh, super quo, (see <reference osisRef="Job.38.6">Job 38:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.10">2Chr 32:10</reference>), upon what part. And so Abendana on Sal. Den Melech: "There are some who explain it thus: Upon what limb shall you be smitten, if you add defection? for already for your sins have you been smitten upon all of them; so that there is not to be found in you a whole limb on which you can be smitten." Which agrees with what follows: "From the sole of the foot even unto the head, there is no soundness in it:" and the sentiment and image is exactly the same with that of Ovid, Pont. 2:7, 42: - <div eID="gen26350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26351" type="x-p"/> Vix habet in nobis jam nova plaga locum. <div eID="gen26351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26352" type="x-p"/> There is no place on you for a new stripe. Or that still more expressive line of Euripides; the great force and effect of which Longinus ascribes to its close and compressed structure, analogous to the sense which it expresses: - ́γεμω κακων δη· κ' ουκετ' εσθ' ὁπη τιθῃ. <div eID="gen26352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26353" type="x-p"/> I am full of miseries: there's no room for more. <div eID="gen26353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26354" type="x-p"/> Herc. Fur. 1245, Long. sec. 40. "On what part will ye strike again? will ye add correction?" This is addressed to the instruments of God's vengeance; those that inflicted the punishment, who or whatsoever they were. Ad verbum certae personae intelligendae sunt, quibus ista actio quae per verbum exprimitur competit; "The words are addressed to the persons who were the agents employed in the work expressed by the original word," as Glassius says in a similar case, Philippians Sacr. 1:3, 22. See <reference osisRef="Isa.7.4">Isa 7:4</reference>. <div eID="gen26354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26355" type="x-p"/> As from ידע yada, דעה deah, knowledge; from יעץ yaats, עצה etsah, counsel; from ישן yeshan, שנה shenah, sleep, etc.; so from יסר yasar is regularly derived סרה sarah, correction. <div eID="gen26355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26356" type="x-p"/> The whole head is sick - The king and the priests are equally gone away from truth and righteousness. Or, The state is oppressed by its enemies, and the Church corrupted in its rulers and in its members.
entries.31d65e19b24b85a2219654ddf1092c7a3c83c649: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26357" type="x-p"/> They have not been closed, etc. "It hath not been pressed," etc. - The pharmaceutical art in the East consists chiefly in external applications: accordingly the prophet's images in this place are all taken from surgery. Sir John Chardin, in his note on <reference osisRef="Pro.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, "It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones," observes that "the comparison is taken from the plasters, ointments, oils, and frictions, which are made use of in the East upon the belly and stomach in most maladies. Being ignorant in the villages of the art of making decoctions and potions, and of the proper doses of such things, they generally make use of external medicines." - Harmer's Observations on Scripture, vol. 2 p. 488. And in surgery their materia medica is extremely simple, oil making the principal part of it. "In India," says Tavernier, "they have a certain preparation of oil and melted grease, which they commonly use for the healing of wounds." Voyage Ind. So the good Samaritan poured oil and wine on the wounds of the distressed Jew: wine, cleansing and somewhat astringent, proper for a fresh wound; oil, mollifying and healing, <reference osisRef="Luk.10.34">Luk 10:34</reference>. Kimchi has a judicious remark here: "When various medicines are applied, and no healing takes place, that disorder is considered as coming immediately from God." <div eID="gen26357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26358" type="x-p"/> Of the three verbs in this sentence, one is in the singular number in the text; another is singular in two MSS., (one of them ancient), חבשה chubbeshah; and the Syriac and Vulgate render all of them in the singular number.
entries.3e51265392489b47c6764127186ce36b129fe4e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26359" type="x-p"/> Your country is desolate - The description of the ruined and desolate state of the country in these verses does not suit with any part of the prosperous times of Uzziah and Jotham. It very well agrees with the time of Ahaz, when Judea was ravaged by the joint invasion of the Israelites and Syrians, and by the incursions of the Philistines and Edomites. The date of this prophecy is therefore generally fixed to the time of Ahaz. But on the other hand it may be considered whether those instances of idolatry which are urged in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference> - the worshipping in groves and gardens - having been at all times too commonly practiced, can be supposed to be the only ones which the prophet would insist upon in the time of Ahaz; who spread the grossest idolatry through the whole country, and introduced it even into the temple; and, to complete his abominations, made his son pass through the fire to Molech. It is said, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37">2Kgs 15:37</reference>, that in Jotham's time "the Lord began to send against Judah Rezin - and Pekah." If we may suppose any invasion from that quarter to have been actually made at the latter end of Jotham's reign, I should choose to refer this prophecy to that time. <div eID="gen26359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26360" type="x-p"/> And your cities are burned. - Nineteen of Dr. Kennicott's MSS. and twenty-two of De Rossi's, some of my own, with the Syriac and Arabic, add the conjunction which makes the hemistich more complete. <div eID="gen26360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26361" type="x-p"/> At the end of the verse, זרים zarim. This reading, though confirmed by all the ancient versions, gives us no good sense; for "your land is devoured by strangers; and is desolate, as if overthrown by strangers," is a mere tautology, or, what is as bad, an identical comparison. Aben Ezra thought that the word in its present form might be taken for the same with זרם zerem, an inundation: Schultens is of the same opinion; (see Taylor's Concord.); and Schindler in his Lexicon explains it in the same manner: and so, says Zimchi, some explain it. Abendana endeavors to reconcile it to grammatical analogy in the following manner: "זרים zarim is the same with זרם zerem; that is, as overthrown by an inundation of waters: and these two words have the same analogy as קדם kedem and קדים kadim. Or it may be a concrete of the same form with שכיר shechir; and the meaning will be: as overthrown by rain pouring down violently, and causing a flood." On Sal. ben Melech, in loc. But I rather suppose the true reading to be זרם zerem, and have translated it accordingly: the word זרים zerim, in the line above, seems to have caught the transcriber's eye, and to have led him into this mistake. But this conjecture of the learned prelate is not confirmed by any MS. yet discovered.
entries.09eb816a86012c756bf1f9e76516267484c9e6fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26362" type="x-p"/> As a cottage in a vineyard "As a shed in a vineyard" - A little temporary hut covered with boughs, straw, turf, or the like materials, for a shelter from the heat by day, and the cold and dews by night, for the watchman that kept the garden or vineyard during the short season the fruit was ripening, (see <reference osisRef="Job.27.18">Job 27:18</reference>), and presently removed when it had served that purpose. See Harmer's Observ. 1:454. They were probably obliged to have such a constant watch to defend the fruit from the jackals. "The jackal," (chical of the Turks), says Hasselquist, (Travels, p. 227), "is a species of mustela which is very common in Palestine, especially during the vintage; and often destroys whole vineyards, and gardens of cucumbers." "There is also plenty of the canis vulpes, the fox, near the convent of St. John in the desert, about vintage time; for they destroy all the vines unless they are strictly watched." Ibid. p. 184. See <reference osisRef="Sol.2.15">Sol 2:15</reference>. <div eID="gen26362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26363" type="x-p"/> Fruits of the gourd kind, melons, watermelons, cucumbers, etc., are much used and in great request in the Levant, on account of their cooling quality. The Israelites in the wilderness regretted the loss of the cucumbers and melons among the other good things of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Num.11.5">Num 11:5</reference>. In Egypt the season of watermelons, which are most in request, and which the common people then chiefly live upon, lasts but three weeks. See Hasselquist, p. 256. Tavernier makes it of longer continuance: <div eID="gen26363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> L'on y void de grands carreaux de melons et de concombres, mais beaucoup plus de derniers, dont les Levantins font leur delices. Le plus souvent, ils les mangent sans les peter, apres quoi ils vont boire une verre d'eau. Dans toute l'Asie c'est la nourriture ordinaire du petit peuple pendant trois ou quatre mois; toute la famine en vit, et quand un enfant demand a manger, au lieu qu'en France ou aillieurs nous luy donnerions du pain, dans le Levant on luy presente un concombre, qu'il mange cru comme on le vient de cueillir. Les concombres dans le Levant ont une bonte particuliere; et quoiqu' on les mange crus, ils ne font jamais de mal; "There are to be seen great beds of melons and cucumbers, but a greater number of the latter, of which the Levantines are particularly fond. In general they eat them without taking off the rind, after which they drink a glass of water. In every part of Asia this is the aliment of the common people for three or four months; the whole family live on them; and when a child asks something to eat, instead of giving it a piece of bread, as is done in France and other countries, they present it with a cucumber, which it eats raw, as gathered. Cucumbers in the Levant are peculiarly excellent; and although eaten raw, they are seldom injurious." Tavernier, Relat. du Serrail, cap. xix. <div eID="gen26364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26365" type="x-p"/> As a lodge, etc. - That is, after the fruit was gathered; the lodge being then permitted to fall into decay. Such was the desolate, ruined state of the city. <div eID="gen26365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26366" type="x-p"/> So the ὡς πολις πολιορκουμενη; Septuagint: see also the Vulgate.
entries.e73f7b6b9ff437a287b5b07428cc612888318f54: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26367" type="x-p"/> The Lord of hosts "Jehovah God of hosts" - As this title of God, יהוה צבאות Yehovah tsebaoth, "Jehovah of hosts, occurs here for the first time, I think it proper to note, that I translate it always, as in this place, "Jehovah God of hosts;" taking it as an elliptical expression for יהוה אלהי צבאות Yehovah Elohey tsebaoth. This title imports that Jehovah is the God or Lord of hosts or armies; as he is the Creator and Supreme Governor of all beings in heaven and earth, and disposeth and ruleth them all in their several orders and stations; the almighty, universal Lord. <div eID="gen26367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26368" type="x-p"/> We should have been as Sodom - As completely and finally ruined as that and the cities of the plain were, no vestige of which remains at this day.
entries.aae7eb331829c80f3ebb5a0a0c201076fe17e009: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen26368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26369" type="x-p"/> Ye rulers of Sodom "Ye princes of Sodom" - The incidental mention of Sodom and Gomorrah in the preceding verse suggested to the prophet this spirited address to the rulers and inhabitants of Jerusalem, under the character of princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah. Two examples of a sort of elegant turn of the like kind may be observed in St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.4">Rom 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.5">Rom 15:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Rom 15:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.13">Rom 15:13</reference>. See Locke on the place; and see <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.30">Isa 1:30</reference>, of this chapter, which gives another example of the same. <div eID="gen26369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26370" type="x-p"/> And - like unto Gomorrah. - The ו vau is added by thirty-one of Kennicott's MSS., twenty-nine of De Rossi's and one, very ancient, of my own. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa 1:6</reference> (note).
entries.9370e64159a36be57a01df0ed0daae795bd50415: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26371" type="x-p"/> To what purpose, etc. "What have I to do" - The prophet Amos has expressed the same sentiments with great elegance: - <div eID="gen26371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26372" type="x-p"/> I hate, I despise your feasts; <div eID="gen26372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26373" type="x-p"/> And I will not delight in the odour of your solemnities: <div eID="gen26373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26374" type="x-p"/> Though ye offer unto me burnt-offerings <div eID="gen26374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26375" type="x-p"/> And your meat-offerings, I will not accept: <div eID="gen26375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26376" type="x-p"/> Neither will I regard the peace-offerings of your fatlings. <div eID="gen26376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26377" type="x-p"/> Take away from me the noise of your songs; <div eID="gen26377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26378" type="x-p"/> And the melody of your viols I will not hear. <div eID="gen26378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26379" type="x-p"/> But let judgment roll down like waters; <div eID="gen26379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26380" type="x-p"/> And righteousness like a mighty stream. <reference osisRef="Amo.5.21-Amo.5.24">Amo 5:21-24</reference>. <div eID="gen26380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26381" type="x-p"/> So has Persius; see Sat. 2 v. 71-75: - "Quin damus id Superis, de magna quod dare lanae," etc. <div eID="gen26381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26382" type="x-p"/> The two or three last pages of Plato's Euthyphro contain the same idea. Sacrifices and prayers are not profitable to the offerer, nor acceptable to the gods, unless accompanied with an upright life. <div eID="gen26382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26383" type="x-p"/> The fat of fed beasts, etc. - The fat and the blood are particularly mentioned, because these were in all sacrifices set apart to God. The fat was always burnt upon the altar, and the blood was partly sprinkled, differently on different occasions, and partly poured out at the bottom of the altar. See Leviticus 4.
entries.ad054c8e4eb32e549db17e38bef4f1019e4d2c5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26384" type="x-p"/> When ye come to appear - Instead of לראות leraoth, to appear, one MS. has לראות liroth, to see. See De Rossi. The appearing before God here refers chiefly to the three solemn annual festivals. See <reference osisRef="Exo.23.14">Exo 23:14</reference>. <div eID="gen26384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26385" type="x-p"/> Tread my courts (no more) - So the Septuagint divide the sentence, joining the end of this verse to the beginning of the next: Πατειν την αυλην μου, ου προσθησεσθε; "To tread my court ye shall not add - ye shall not be again accepted in worship."
entries.7e9ee87bb14077bd4f1bbba69b81a7d5f9357be6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26386" type="x-p"/> The new moons and Sabbaths "The fast and the day of restraint" - און ועצרה aven vaatsarah. These words are rendered in many different manners by different interpreters, to a good and probable sense by all; but I think by none in such a sense as can arise from the phrase itself, agreeably to the idiom of the Hebrew language. Instead of און aven, the Septuagint manifestly read צום tsom, νηστειαν, "the fast." This Houbigant has adopted. The prophet could not well have omitted the fast in the enumeration of their solemnities, nor the abuse of it among the instances of their hypocrisy, which he has treated at large with such force and elegance in his fifty-eighth chapter. Observe, also, that the prophet Joel, (<reference osisRef="Joe.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Joe.2.15">Joe 2:15</reference>), twice joins together the fast and the day of restraint: - עצרה קראו צום קדשו atsarah kiru tsom kaddeshu "Sanctify a fast; proclaim a day of restraint:" which shows how properly they are here joined together. עצרה atsarah, "the restraint," is rendered, both here and in other places of our English translation, "the solemn assembly." Certain holy days ordained by the law were distinguished by a particular charge that "no servile work should be done therein;" <reference osisRef="Lev.23.36">Lev 23:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.29.35">Num 29:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.16.8">Deu 16:8</reference>. This circumstance clearly explains the reason of the name, the restraint, or the day of restraint, given to those days. <div eID="gen26386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26387" type="x-p"/> If I could approve of any translation of these two words which I have met with, it should be that of the Spanish version of the Old Testament, made for the use of the Spanish Jews: Tortura y detenimento, "it is a pain and a constraint unto me." But I still think that the reading of the Septuagint is more probably the truth.
entries.e7676300165faf4de27a6aa07c01e9222446c85b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen26387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26388" type="x-p"/> When ye spread - The Syriac, Septuagint, and a MS., read בפרשכם beparshecem, without the conjunction ו vau. <div eID="gen26388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26389" type="x-p"/> Your hands "For your hands" - Αἱ γαρ χειρες - Sept. Manus enim vestrae-Vulg. They seem to have read כי ידיכם ki yedeychem.
entries.4904a0d91faeaeeaaa3c48d87c890702c941ca27: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen26389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26390" type="x-p"/> Wash you - Referring to the preceding verse, "your hands are full of blood;" and alluding to the legal washing commanded on several occasions. See <reference osisRef="Lev.14.8">Lev 14:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.9">Lev 14:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.47">Lev 14:47</reference>.
entries.292befd79a5c90ca15e657b5ac316e5e9d4a8e0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen26390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26391" type="x-p"/> Relieve the oppressed "Amend that which is corrupted" - אשרו חמוץ asheru chamots. In rendering this obscure phrase I follow Bochart, (Hieroz. Part i., lib. ii., cap. 7), though I am not perfectly satisfied with this explication of it.
entries.14611d26c99a1a272b569fdc4fa5b825357fc371: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen26391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26392" type="x-p"/> Though your sins be as scarlet - שני shani, "scarlet or crimson," dibaphum, twice dipped, or double dyed; from שנה shanah, iterare, to double, or to do a thing twice. This derivation seems much more probable than that which Salmasius prefers from שנן shanan, acuere, to whet, from the sharpness and strength of the color, οξυφοινικον; תלע tela, the same; properly the worm, vermiculus, (from whence vermeil), for this color was produced from a worm or insect which grew in a coccus or excrescence of a shrub of the ilex kind, (see Plin. Nat. Hist. 16:8), like the cochineal worm in the opuntia of America. See Ulloa's Voyage book v., chap. ii., note to page 342. There is a shrub of this kind that grows in Provence and Languedoc, and produces the like insect, called the kermes oak, (see Miller, Dict. Quercus), from kermez, the Arabic word for this color, whence our word crimson is derived. "Neque amissos colores <div eID="gen26392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26393" type="x-p"/> Lana refert medicata fuco," says the poet, applying the same image to a different purpose. To discharge these strong colors is impossible to human art or power; but to the grace and power of God all things, even much more difficult are possible and easy. Some copies have כשנים keshanim, "like crimson garments." <div eID="gen26393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26394" type="x-p"/> Though they be red, etc. - But the conjunction ו vau is added by twenty-one of Kennicott's, and by forty-two of De Rossi's MSS., by some early editions, with the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic. It makes a fuller and more emphatic sense. "And though they be red as crimson," etc.
entries.95f26392156226af79a04c81eb5f2d9bc89be207: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen26394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26395" type="x-p"/> Ye shall eat the good of the land - Referring to <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7">Isa 1:7</reference> : it shall not be "devoured by strangers."
entries.270496d953d7925ac5b6f4005413eccad896dad7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen26395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26396" type="x-p"/> Ye shall be devoured with the sword "Ye shall be food for the sword" - The Septuagint and Vulgate read תאכלכם tochalchem, "the sword shall devour you;" which is of much more easy construction than the present reading of the text. <div eID="gen26396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26397" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee seems to read בחרב אויב תאכלו bechereb oyeb teachelu, "ye shall be consumed by the sword of the enemy." The Syriac also reads בחרב beehereb and renders the verb passively. And the rhythmus seems to require this addition. - Dr. Jubb.
entries.f9d51df4f45c6613054d0f22e8bfe9a1fe3473ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen26397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26398" type="x-p"/> Become a harlot - See before, the Discourse on the Prophetic Style; and see Lowth's Comment on the place, and De Sacr. Poes. Hebr. Prael. xxxi.
entries.842e1a3e8357b723b99f93b320277ba2e405ac9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen26398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26399" type="x-p"/> Wine mixed with water - An image used for the adulteration of wines, with more propriety than may at first appear, if what Thevenot says of the people of the Levant of late times were true of them formerly. He says, "They never mingle water with their wine to drink; but drink by itself what water they think proper for abating the strength of the wine." "Lorsque les Persans boivent du vin, ils le prennent tout pur, a la facon des Levantins, qui ne le melent jamais avec de l'eua; mais en beuvant du vin, de temps en temps ils prennent un pot d'eau, et en boivent de grand traits." Voyage, part ii., 54 ii., chap. 10. "Ils (les Turcs) n'y meslent jamais d'eau, et se moquent des Chretiens qui en mettent, ce qui leur semble tout a fait ridicule." Ibid. part i., chap. 24. "The Turks never mingle water with their wine, and laugh at the Christians for doing it, which they consider altogether ridiculous." <div eID="gen26399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26400" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable that whereas the Greeks and Latins by mixed wine always understood wine diluted and lowered with water, the Hebrews on the contrary generally mean by it wine made stronger and more inebriating by the addition of higher and more powerful ingredients, such as honey, spices, defrutum, (or wine inspissated by boiling it down to two-thirds or one-half of the quantity), myrrh, mandragora, opiates, and other strong drugs. Such were the exhilarating, or rather stupefying, ingredients which Helen mixed in the bowl together with the wine for her guests oppressed with grief to raise their spirits, the composition of which she had learned in Egypt: - Αυτικ' αρ' εις οινον βαλε φαρμακον, ενθεν επινον, Νηπενθες τ' αχολον τε, κακων επιληθον ἁπαντων. <div eID="gen26400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26401" type="x-p"/> Homer. Odyss. lib. iv., ver. 220.
