The omnipotence of God had mercifully preserved it: <hi type="italic">“Unless Jehovah of hosts had left us a little of what had escaped, we had become like Sodom, we were like Gomorrah.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Sarid</hi> (which is rendered inaccurately σπέρμα in the Sept.; cf., <reference osisRef="Rom.9.29">Rom 9:29</reference>) was used, even in the early Mosaic usage of the language, to signify that which escaped the general destruction (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.34">Deu 2:34</reference>, etc.); and כּמעט (which might very well be connected with the verbs which follow: “we were very nearly within a little like Sodom,” etc.) is to be taken in connection with <hi type="italic">sarid</hi>, as the pausal form clearly shows: “a remnant which was but a mere trifle” (on this use of the word, see <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.7">2Ch 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.20">Pro 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.12">Psa 105:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Jehovah Zebaoth</hi> stands first, for the sake of emphasis. It would have been all over with Israel long ago, if it had not been for the compassion of God (vid., Hos 11:8). And because it was the omnipotence of God, which set the will of His compassion in motion, He is called <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> <hi type="italic">Zebaoth</hi>, Jehovah (the God) of the heavenly hosts - an expression in which <hi type="italic">Zebaoth</hi> is a dependent genitive, and not, as Luzzatto supposes, an independent name of God as the Absolute, embracing within itself all the powers of nature. The prophet says “us” and “we.” He himself was an inhabitant of Jerusalem; and even if he had not been so, he was nevertheless an Israelite. He therefore associates himself with his people, like Jeremiah in Lam 3:22. He had had to experience the anger of God along with the rest; and so, on the other hand, he also celebrates the mighty compassion of God, which he had experienced in common with them. But for this compassion, the people of God would have become like Sodom, from which only four human beings escaped: it would have resembled Gomorrah, which was absolutely annihilated. (On the prefects in the protasis and apodosis, see Ges. §126, 5.)
entries.bad755310faeaead926134af5fceeeaa36fd98b7: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10-Isa.1.11">Isa 1:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen12785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12786" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s address has here reached a resting-place. The fact that it is divided at this point into two separate sections, is indicated in the text by the space left between <reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Isa 1:9</reference> and Isa 1:10. This mode of marking larger or smaller sections, either by leaving spaces of by breaking off the line, is older than the vowel points and accents, and rests upon a tradition of the highest antiquity (Hupfeld, <hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. p. 86ff.). The space is called <hi type="italic">pizka</hi>; the section indicated by such a space, a closed <hi type="italic">parashah</hi> (<hi type="italic">sethumah</hi>); and the section indicated by breaking off the line, an open <hi type="italic">parashah</hi> (<hi type="italic">petuchah</hi>). The prophet stops as soon as he has affirmed, that nothing but the mercy of God has warded off from Israel the utter destruction which it so well deserved. He catches in spirit the remonstrances of his hearers. They would probably declare that the accusations which the prophet had brought against them were utterly groundless, and appeal to their scrupulous observance of the law of God. In reply to this self-vindication which he reads in the hearts of the accused, the prophet launches forth the accusations of God. In <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa 1:11</reference>, he commences thus: <hi type="italic">“Hear the word of Jehovah, ye Sodom judges; give ear to the law of our God, O Gomorrah nation! What is the multitude of your slain-offerings to me? saith Jehovah. I am satiated with whole offerings of rams, and the fat of stalled calves; and blood of bullocks and sheep and he-goats I do not like.”</hi> The second start in the prophet’s address commences, like the first, with “hear” and “give ear.” The summons to hear is addressed in this instances (as in the case of Isaiah’s contemporary Micah, Mic 3:1-12) to the <hi type="italic">kezinim</hi> (from <hi type="italic">kâzâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">decidere</hi>, from which comes the Arabic <hi type="italic">el - Kadi</hi>, the judge, with the substantive termination <hi type="italic">in</hi>: see <hi type="italic">Jeshurun</hi>, p. 212 ss.), i.e., to the men of decisive authority, the rulers in the broadest sense, and to the people subject to them. It was through the mercy of God that Jerusalem was in existence still, for Jerusalem was “spiritually Sodom,” as the Revelation (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Rev 11:8</reference>) distinctly affirms of Jerusalem, with evident allusion to this passage of Isaiah. Pride, lust of the flesh, and unmerciful conduct, were the leading sins of Sodom, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.49">Eze 16:49</reference>; and of these, the rulers of Jerusalem, and the crowd that was subject to them and worthy of them, were equally guilty now. But they fancied that they could not possibly stand in such evil repute with God, inasmuch as they rendered outward satisfaction to the law. The prophet therefore called upon them to hear the law of the God of Israel, which he would announce to them: for the prophet was the appointed interpreter of the law, and prophecy the spirit of the law, and the prophetic institution the constant living presence of the true essence of the law bearing its own witness in Israel. “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith Jehovah.” The prophet intentionally uses the word יאמר, not אמר: this was the incessant appeal of God in relation to the spiritless, formal worship offered by the hypocritical, ceremonial righteousness of Israel (the future denoting continuous actions, which is ever at the same time both present and future). The multitude of <hi type="italic">zebâchim</hi>, i.e., animal sacrifices, had no worth at all to Him. As the whole worship is summed up here in one single act, <hi type="italic">zebâchim</hi> appears to denote the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi>, peace-offerings (or better still, communion offerings), with which a meal was associated, after the style of a sacrificial festival, and Jehovah gave the worshipper a share in the sacrifice offered. It is better, however, to take <hi type="italic">zebâchim</hi> as the general name for all the bleeding sacrifices, which are then subdivided into <hi type="italic">'oloth</hi> and <hi type="italic">Cheleb</hi>, as consisting partly of whole offerings, or offerings the whole of which was placed upon the altar, though in separate pieces, and entirely consumed, and partly of those sacrifices in which only the fat was consumed upon the altar, namely the sin-offerings, trespass-offerings, and pre-eminently the <hi type="italic">shelâmim</hi> offerings. Of the sacrificial animals mentioned, the bullocks (<hi type="italic">pârim</hi>) and fed beasts (<hi type="italic">meri'im</hi>, fattened calves) are species of oxen (<hi type="italic">bakar</hi>); and the lambs (<hi type="italic">Cebashim</hi>) and he-goats (<hi type="italic">atturim</hi>, young he-goats, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">se'ir</hi>, the old long-haired he-goat, the animal used as a sin-offering), together with the ram (<hi type="italic">ayil</hi>, the customary whole offering of the high priest, of the tribe prince, and of the nation generally on all the high feast days), were species of the flock. The blood of these sacrificial animals - such, for example, as the young oxen, sheep, and he-goats - was thrown all round the altar in the case of the whole offering, the peace-offering, and the trespass-offering; in that of the sin-offering it was smeared upon the horns of the altar, poured out at the foot of the altar, and in some instances sprinkled upon the walls of the altar, or against the vessels of the inner sanctuary. Of such offerings as these Jehovah was weary, and He wanted no more (the two perfects denote that which long has been and still is: Ges. §126, 3); in fact, He never had desired anything of the kind.
entries.c0fbc6df50f6db70a91f51bdc4b73ddd8700e3d3: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.12">Isa 1:12</reference> <div eID="gen12786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12787" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah says this with regard to the sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">Isa 7:22</reference>); Isaiah also applies it to visits to the temple: <hi type="italic">“When ye come to appear before my face, who hath required this at your hand, to tread my courts?”</hi> לראות is a contracted infinitive <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> for להראות (compare the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> forms contracted in the same manner in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8">Isa 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">Isa 23:11</reference>). This is the standing expression for the appearance of all male Israelites in the temple at the three high festivals, as prescribed by the law, and then for visits to the temple generally (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.8">Psa 84:8</reference>). “My face” (<hi type="italic">panai</hi>): according to Ewald, §279, c, this is used with the passive to designate the subject (“to be seen by the face of God”); but why not rather take it as an adverbial accusative, “in the face of,” or “in front of,” as it is used interchangeably with the prepositions ל, את, and אל? It is possible that לראות is pointed as it is here, and in <reference osisRef="Exod.34.24">Exo 34:24</reference> and in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">Deu 31:11</reference>, instead of לראות - like יראוּ for יראוּ, in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">Exo 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.20">Exo 34:20</reference>, - for the purpose of avoiding an expression which might be so easily misunderstood as denoting a sight of God with the bodily eye. But the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> is firmly established in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Exo 23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.23">Exo 34:23</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.22">1Sa 1:22</reference>; and in the Mishnah and Talmud the terms ראיה and ראיון are applied without hesitation to appearance before God at the principal feasts. They visited the temple diligently enough indeed, but who had required <hi type="italic">this</hi> at their hand, i.e., required them to do this? Jehovah certainly had not. “<hi type="italic">To tread my courts</hi>” is in apposition to <hi type="italic">this</hi>, which it more clearly defines. Jehovah did not want them to appear before His face, i.e., He did not wish for this spiritless and undevotional tramping thither, this mere <hi type="italic">opus operatum</hi>, which might as well have been omitted, since it only wore out the floor.
entries.91e6721a1270ddfde6754f71026d318bd915b15a: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference> <div eID="gen12787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12788" type="x-p"/> Because they had not performed what Jehovah commanded as He commanded it, He expressly forbids them to continue it. <hi type="italic">“Continue not to bring lying meat-offering; abomination incense is it to me.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Minchah</hi> (the meat-offering) was the vegetable offering, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">zebach</hi>, the animal sacrifice. It is called a “lying meat-offering,” as being a hypocritical dead work, behind which there was none of the feeling which it appeared to express. In the second clause the Sept., Vulg., Gesenius, and others adopt the rendering “incense - an abomination is it to me,” <hi type="italic">ketoreth</hi> being taken as the name of the daily burning of incense upon the golden altar in the holy place (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.8">Exo 30:8</reference>). But neither in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>, where prayer is offered by one who is not a priest, nor in the passage before us, where the reference is not to the priesthood, but to the people and to their deeds, is this continual incense to be thought of. Moreover, it is much more natural to regard the word <hi type="italic">ketoreth</hi> not as a bold absolute case, but, according to the conjunctive <hi type="italic">darga</hi> with which it is marked, as constructive rather; and this is perfectly allowable. The meat-offering is called “incense” (<hi type="italic">ketoreth</hi>) with reference to the so-called <hi type="italic">azcarah</hi>, i.e., that portion which the priest burned upon the altar, to bring the grateful offerer into remembrance before God (called “burning the memorial,” <hi type="italic">hiktir</hi> <hi type="italic">azcârâh</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Lev.2.2">Lev 2:2</reference>). As a general rule, this was accompanied with incense (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>), the whole of which was placed upon the altar, and not merely a small portion of it. The meat-offering, with its sweet-smelling savour, was merely the form, which served as an outward expression of the thanksgiving for God’s blessing, or the longing for His blessing, which really ascended in prayer. But in their case the form had no such meaning. It was nothing but the form, with which they thought they had satisfied God; and therefore it was an abomination to Him. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference></hi>. God was just as little pleased with their punctilious observance of the feasts: <hi type="italic">“New-moon and Sabbath, calling of festal meetings ... I cannot bear ungodliness and a festal crowd.”</hi> The first objective notions, which are logically governed by “I cannot bear” (לא־אוּכל: literally, a future <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> - I am unable, incapable, viz., to bear, which may be supplied, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">Jer 44:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.21">Pro 30:21</reference>), become <hi type="italic">absolute cases</hi> here, on account of another grammatical object presenting itself in the last two nouns: “ungodliness and a festal crowd.” As for new-moon and Sabbath (the latter always signifies the weekly Sabbath when construed with <hi type="italic">Chodesh</hi>) - and, in fact, the calling of meetings of the whole congregation on the weekly Sabbath and high festivals, which was a simple duty according to Lev 23 - - Jehovah could not endure festivals associated with wickedness. עצרה (from עצר, to press, or crowd thickly together) is synonymous with מקרא), so far as its immediate signification is concerned, as <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer 9:1</reference> clearly shows, just as πανήγυρις is synonymous with εκκλησία . און (from אוּן, to breathe) is moral worthlessness, regarded as an utter absence of all that has true essence and worth in the sight of God. The prophet intentionally joins these two nouns together. A densely crowded festal meeting, combined with inward emptiness and barrenness on the part of those who were assembled together, was a contradiction which God could not endure.
entries.98f029ccd1b479302f191e534dc3ff9acbffb3ea: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.14">Isa 1:14</reference> <div eID="gen12788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12789" type="x-p"/> He gives a still stronger expression to His repugnance: <hi type="italic">“Your new-moons and your festive seasons my soul hateth; they have become a burden to me; I am weary of bearing them.”</hi> As the soul (<hi type="italic">nephesh</hi>) of a man, regarded as the band which unites together bodily and spiritual life, though it is not the actual principle of self-consciousness, is yet the place in which he draws, as it were, the circle of self-consciousness, so as to comprehend the whole essence of His being in the single thought of “I;” so, according to a description taken from godlike man, the “soul” (<hi type="italic">nephesh</hi>) of God, as the expression “my soul” indicates, is the centre of His being, regarded as encircled and pervaded (personated) by self-consciousness; and therefore, whatever the soul of God hates (vid., <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">Jer 15:1</reference>) or loves (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa 42:1</reference>), is hated or loved in the inmost depths and to the utmost bounds of His being (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 218). Thus He hated each and all of the festivals that were kept in Jerusalem, whether the beginnings of the month, or the high feast-days (<hi type="italic">moadim</hi>, in which, according to Lev 23, the Sabbath was also included) observed in the course of the month. For a long time past they had become a burden and annoyance to Him: His long-suffering was weary of such worship. <hi type="italic">“To bear”</hi> (נשׂא), in Isaiah, even in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">Isa 18:3</reference>, for שׂאת or שׂאת ro , and here for לשׂאת: Ewald, §285,<hi type="italic">c</hi>) has for its object the seasons of worship already mentioned.
entries.2f45d4f12de8522115ae5a3ed58824920cad8ed0: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa 1:15</reference> <div eID="gen12789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12790" type="x-p"/> Their self-righteousness, so far as it rested upon sacrifices and festal observances, was now put to shame, and the last inward bulwark of the sham holy nation was destroyed: <hi type="italic">“And if ye stretch out your hands, I hide my eyes from you; if ye make ever so much praying, I do not hear: your hands are full of blood.”</hi> Their praying was also an abomination to God. Prayer is something common to man: it is the interpreter of religious feeling, which intervenes and mediates between God and man;<note placement="foot">The primary idea of <hi type="italic">hithpallel</hi> and <hi type="italic">tephillah</hi> is not to be obtained from <reference osisRef="Deut.9.18">Deu 9:18</reference> and Ezr 10:1, as Dietrich and Fürst suppose, who make <hi type="italic">hithpallel</hi> equivalent to <hi type="italic">hithnappel</hi>, to throw one’s self down; but from <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.25">1Sa 2:25</reference>, “If a man sin against a man, the authorities right him” (וּפללו אלהים: it is quite a mistake to maintain that <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> cannot have this meaning), i.e., they can set right the relation which he has disturbed. “But if one sin against Jehovah, who shall mediate for him (מי יתפּלּל־לו, <hi type="italic">quis intercedat pro eo</hi>)?” We may see from this that prayer is regarded as mediation, which sets right and establishes fellowship; and <hi type="italic">hithpallel</hi> signifies to make one’s self a healer of divisions, or to settle for one’s self, to strive after a settlement (<hi type="italic">sibi</hi>, <hi type="italic">pro se</hi>, <hi type="italic">intercedere</hi>: cf., <reference osisRef="Job.19.16">Job 19:16</reference>, <hi type="italic">hithchannen</hi>, <hi type="italic">sibi propitium facere</hi>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>, <hi type="italic">hithchakkah</hi>, <hi type="italic">sibi insculpere</hi>, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">ichtatta</hi>, to bound off for one’s self).</note> it is the true spiritual sacrifice. The law contains no command to pray, and, with the exception of Deut 26, no form of prayer. Praying is so natural to man as man, that there was no necessity for any precept to enforce this, the fundamental expression of the true relation to God. The prophet therefore comes to prayer last of all, so as to trace back their sham-holiness, which was corrupt even to this the last foundation, to its real nothingness. “Spread out,” <hi type="italic">parash</hi>, or <hi type="italic">pi pērēsh</hi>, to stretch out; used with <hi type="italic">Cappaim</hi> to denote swimming in Isa 25:11. It is written here before a strong suffix, as in many other passages, e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Isa 52:12</reference>, with the inflection <hi type="italic">i</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">e</hi>. This was the gesture of a man in prayer, who spread out his hands, and when spread out, stretched them towards heaven, or to the most holy place in the temple, and indeed (as if with the feeling of emptiness and need, and with a desire to receive divine gifts) held up the hollow or palm of his hand (<hi type="italic">Cappaim</hi>: cf., <hi type="italic">tendere palmas</hi>, e.g., Virg. <hi type="italic">Aen</hi>. xii. 196, <hi type="italic">tenditque ad sidera palmas</hi>). However much they might stand or lie before Him in the attitude of prayer, Jehovah hid His eyes, i.e., His omniscience knew nothing of it; and even though they might pray loud and long (<hi type="italic">gam chi</hi>, <hi type="italic">etiamsi</hi>: compare the simple <hi type="italic">Chi</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">Jer 14:12</reference>), He was, as it were, deaf to it all. We should expect <hi type="italic">Chi</hi> here to introduce the explanation; but the more excited the speaker, the shorter and more unconnected his words. The plural <hi type="italic">damim</hi> always denotes human blood as the result of some unnatural act, and then the bloody deed and the bloodguiltiness itself. The plural number neither refers to the quantity nor to the separate drops, but is the plural of production, which Dietrich has so elaborately discussed in his <hi type="italic">Abhandlung</hi>, p. 40.<note placement="foot">As <hi type="italic">Chittah</hi> signified corn standing in the field, and <hi type="italic">Chittim</hi> corn threshed and brought to the market, so <hi type="italic">damim</hi> was not blood when flowing through the veins, but when it had flowed out-in other words, when it had been violently shed. (For the Talmudic misinterpretation of the true state of the case, see my <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 626.)</note> <div eID="gen12790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12791" type="x-p"/> The terrible <hi type="italic">damim</hi> stands very emphatically before the governing verb, pointing to many murderous acts that had been committed, and deeds of violence akin to murder. Not, indeed, that we are to understand the words as meaning that there was really blood upon their hands when they stretched them out in prayer; but before God, from whom no outward show can hide the true nature of things, however clean they might have washed themselves, they still dripped with blood. The expostulations of the people against the divine accusations have thus been negatively set forth and met in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11-Isa.1.15">Isa 1:11-15</reference> : Jehovah could not endure their work-righteous worship, which was thus defiled with unrighteous works, even to murder itself. The divine accusation is now positively established in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.17">Isa 1:17</reference>, by the contrast drawn between the true righteousness of which the accused were destitute, and the false righteousness of which they boasted. The crushing charge is here changed into an admonitory appeal; and the love which is hidden behind the wrath, and would gladly break through, already begins to disclose itself. There are eight admonitions. The first three point to the removal of evil; the other five to the performance of what is good.
entries.62ba39f5f1af28e10b9f26222fd5c36b27aab537: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference> <div eID="gen12791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12792" type="x-p"/> The first three run thus: <hi type="italic">“Wash, clean yourselves; put away the badness of your doings from the range of my eyes; cease to do evil.”</hi> This is not only an advance from figurative language to the most literal, but there is also an advance in what is said. The first admonition requires, primarily and above all, purification from the sins committed, by means of forgiveness sought for and obtained. <hi type="italic">Wash:</hi> <hi type="italic">rachatzu</hi>, from <hi type="italic">râchatz</hi>, in the frequent middle sense of washing one’s self. <hi type="italic">Clean yourselves:</hi> <hi type="italic">hizdaccu</hi>, with the tone upon the last syllable, is not the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> of <hi type="italic">zâkak</hi>, as the first plur. imper. <hi type="italic">niph</hi>. of such verbs has generally and naturally the tone upon the penultimate (see <reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">Isa 52:11</reference>; Num 17:10), but the <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> of <hi type="italic">zacah</hi> for <hi type="italic">hizdaccu</hi>, with the preformative <hi type="italic">Tav</hi> resolved into the first radical letter, as is very common in the <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> (Ges. §54, 2,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). According to the difference between the two synonyms (to wash one’s self, to clean one’s self), the former must be understood as referring to the one great act of repentance on the part of a man who is turning to God, the latter to the daily repentance of one who has so turned. The second admonition requires them to place themselves in the light of the divine countenance, and put away the evil of their doings, which was intolerable to pure eyes (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab 1:13</reference>). They were to wrestle against the wickedness to which their actual sin had grown, until at length it entirely disappeared. <hi type="italic">Neged</hi>, according to its radical meaning, signifies prominence (compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">ne‛gd</hi>, high land which is visible at a great distance), conspicuousness, so that <hi type="italic">minneged</hi> is really equivalent to <hi type="italic">ex apparentia</hi>.
entries.b0162f947d696f64a28137ce224e23d9775afa01: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.17">Isa 1:17</reference> <div eID="gen12792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12793" type="x-p"/> Five admonitions relating to the practice of what is good: <hi type="italic">“Learn to do good, attend to judgment, set the oppressor right, do justice to the orphan, conduct the cause of the widow.”</hi> The first admonition lays the foundation for the rest. They were to learn to do good - a difficult art, in which a man does not become proficient merely by good intentions. “Learn to do good:” <hi type="italic">hetib</hi> is the object to <hi type="italic">limdu</hi> (learn), regarded as an accusative; the inf. abs. הרע in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference> takes the place of the object in just the same manner. The division of this primary admonition into four minor ones relating to the administration of justice, may be explained from the circumstance that no other prophet directs so keen an eye upon the state and its judicial proceedings as Isaiah has done. He differs in this respect from his younger contemporary Micah, whose prophecies are generally more ethical in their nature, whilst those of Isaiah have a political character throughout. Hence the admonitions: <hi type="italic">“Give diligent attention to judgment”</hi> (<hi type="italic">dârash</hi>, to devote one’s self to a thing with zeal and assiduity); and <hi type="italic">“bring the oppressor to the right way.”</hi> This is the true rendering, as <hi type="italic">Châmotz</hi> (from <hi type="italic">Châmatz</hi>, to be sharp in flavour, glaring in appearance, violent and impetuous in character) cannot well mean “the oppressed,” or the man who is deprived of his rights, as most of the early translators have rendered it, since this form of the noun, especially with an immutable <hi type="italic">kametz</hi> like בּגוד בּגודה (cf., נקד נקּדּה), is not used in a passive, but in an active or attributive sense (Ewald, §152, <hi type="italic">b:</hi> vid., at <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>): it has therefore the same meaning as <hi type="italic">Chomeotz</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">Psa 71:4</reference>, and <hi type="italic">âshok</hi> in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jer 22:3</reference>, which is similar in its form. But if <hi type="italic">Châmotz</hi> signifies the oppressive, reckless, churlish man, אשּׁר cannot mean to make happy, or to congratulate, or to set up, or, as in the talmudic rendering, to strengthen (Luzzatto: <hi type="italic">rianimate chi è oppresso</hi>); but, as it is also to be rendered in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">Isa 9:15</reference>, to lead to the straight road, or to cause a person to keep the straight course. In the case before us, where the oppressor is spoken of, it means to direct him to the way of justice, to keep him in bounds by severe punishment and discipline.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> varies in its explanation of <hi type="italic">Chamoz</hi>: in one instance it is applied to a judge who lets his sentence be thoroughly leavened before pronouncing it; in another the <hi type="italic">Chamuz</hi> is said to signify a person robbed and injured, in opposition to <hi type="italic">Chomez</hi> (<hi type="italic">b. Sanhedrin </hi> 35 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). It is an instructive fact in relation to the idea suggested by the word, that, according to <hi type="italic">Joma</hi> 39 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, a man who had not only taken possession of his own inheritance, but had seized upon another person’s also, bore the nickname of <hi type="italic">ben chimzon</hi> as long as he lived.</note> <div eID="gen12793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12794" type="x-p"/> In the same way we find in other passages, such as <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">Psa 72:4</reference>, severe conduct towards oppressors mentioned in connection with just treatment of the poor. There follow two admonitions relating to widows and orphans. Widows and orphans, as well as foreigners, were the <hi type="italic">protégés</hi> of God and His law, standing under His especial guardianship and care (see, for example, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.22">Exo 22:22</reference> (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.21">21</reference>), cf., <reference osisRef="Exod.21.21">Exo 21:21</reference> (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.20">20</reference>). <hi type="italic">“Do justice to the orphan”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Shâphat</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.25.1">Deu 25:1</reference>, is a contracted expression for <hi type="italic">shâphat mishpat</hi>): for if there is not even a settlement or verdict in their cause, this is the most crying injustice of all, as neither the form nor the appearance of justice is preserved. <hi type="italic">“Conduct the cause of the widows:”</hi> ריב with an accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22">Isa 51:22</reference>, the only other passage in which it occurs, is a contracted form for ריב ריב. Thus all the grounds of self-defence, which existed in the hearts of the accused, are both negatively and positively overthrown. They are thundered down and put to shame. The law (<hi type="italic">thorah</hi>), announced in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>, has been preached to them. The prophet has cast away the husks of their dead works, and brought out the moral kernel of the law in its universal application.
entries.7120cacab5455d610ee3e8d1a7b124a835f278dd: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference> <div eID="gen12794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12795" type="x-p"/> The first leading division of the address is brought to a close, and <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference> contains the turning-point between the two parts into which it is divided. Hitherto Jehovah has spoken to His people in wrath. But His love began to move even in the admonitions in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference>, Isa 1:17. And now this love, which desired not Israel’s destruction, but Israel’s inward and outward salvation, breaks fully through. <hi type="italic">“O come, and let us reason together, saith Jehovah. If your sins come forth like scarlet cloth, they shall become white as snow; if they are red as crimson, they shall come forth like wool!”</hi> Jehovah here challenges Israel to a formal trial: <hi type="italic">nocach</hi> is thus used in a reciprocal sense, and with the same meaning as <hi type="italic">nishpat</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Isa 43:26</reference> (Ges. §51, 2). In such a trial Israel must lose, for Israel’s self-righteousness rests upon sham righteousness; and this sham righteousness, when rightly examined, is but unrighteousness dripping with blood. It is taken for granted that this must be the result of the investigation. Israel is therefore worthy of death. Yet Jehovah will not treat Israel according to His retributive justice, but according to His free compassion. He will remit the punishment, and not only regard the sin as not existing, but change it into its very opposite. The reddest possible sin shall become, through His mercy, the purest white. On the two <hi type="italic">hiphils</hi> here applied to colour, see Ges. §53, 2; though he gives the meaning incorrectly, viz., “to take a colour,” whereas the words signify rather to emit a colour: not <hi type="italic">Colorem accipere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">Colorem dare</hi>. <hi type="italic">Shâni</hi>, bright red (the plural <hi type="italic">shânim</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.21">Pro 31:21</reference>, signifies materials dyed with <hi type="italic">shâni</hi>), and <hi type="italic">tolâ</hi>, warm colour, are simply different names for the same colour, viz., the crimson obtained from the cochineal insect, <hi type="italic">Color cocccineus</hi>. The representation of the work of grace promised by God as a change from red to white, is founded upon the symbolism of colours, quite as much as when the saints in the Revelation (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev 19:8</reference>) are described as clothed in white raiment, whilst the clothing of Babylon is purple and scarlet (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.4">Isa 17:4</reference>). Red is the colour of fire, and therefore of life: the blood is red because life is a fiery process. For this reason the heifer, from which the ashes of purification were obtained for those who had been defiled through contact with the dead, was to be red; and the sprinkling-brush, with which the unclean were sprinkled, was to be tied round with a band of scarlet wool. But red as contrasted with white, the colour of light (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.2">Mat 17:2</reference>), is the colour of selfish, covetous, passionate life, which is self-seeking in its nature, which goes out of itself only to destroy, and drives about with wild tempestuous violence: it is therefore the colour of wrath and sin. It is generally supposed that Isaiah speaks of red as the colour of sin, because sin ends in murder; and this is not really wrong, though it is too restricted. Sin is called red, inasmuch as it is a burning heat which consumes a man, and when it breaks forth consumes his fellow-man as well. According to the biblical view, throughout, sin stands in the same relation to what is well-pleasing to God, and wrath in the same relation to love or grace, as fire to light; and therefore as red to white, or black to white, for red and black are colours which border upon one another. In the Song of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.5">Isa 7:5</reference>), the black locks of Shulamith are described as being “like purple,” and Homer applies the same epithet to the dark waves of the sea. But the ground of this relation lies deeper still. Red is the colour of fire, which flashes out of darkness and returns to it again; whereas white without any admixture of darkness represents the pure, absolute triumph of light. It is a deeply significant symbol of the act of justification. Jehovah offers to Israel an <hi type="italic">actio forensis</hi>, out of which it shall come forth justified by grace, although it has merited death on account of its sins. The righteousness, white as snow and wool, with which Israel comes forth, is a gift conferred upon it out of pure compassion, without being conditional upon any legal performance whatever.
entries.8b97bdd19e86c2920c062fe1fe4d94a8c50159c9: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.19-Isa.1.20">Isa 1:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen12795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12796" type="x-p"/> But after the restoration of Israel <hi type="italic">in integrum</hi> by this act of grace, the rest would unquestionably depend upon the conduct of Israel itself. According to Israel’s own decision would Jehovah determine Israel’s future. <hi type="italic">“If ye then shall willingly hear, ye shall eat the good of the land; if ye shall obstinately rebel, ye shall be eaten by the sword: for the mouth of Jehovah hath spoken it.”</hi> After their justification, both blessing and cursing lay once more before the justified, as they had both been long before proclaimed by the law (compare <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.19">Isa 1:19</reference></hi> with Deu 28:3., Lev 26:3., and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.1.20">Isa 1:20</reference></hi> with the threat of vengeance with the sword in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.25">Lev 26:25</reference>). The promise of eating, i.e., of the full enjoyment of domestic blessings, and therefore of settled, peaceful rest at home, is placed in contrast with the curse of being eaten with the sword. <hi type="italic">Chereb</hi> (the sword) is the accusative of the instrument, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Psa 17:13-14</reference>; but this adverbial construction without either genitive, adjective, or suffix, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.30.20">Exo 30:20</reference>, is very rarely met with (Ges. §138, Anm. 3); and in the passage before us it is a bold construction which the prophet allows himself, instead of saying, חרב תּאכלכם, for the sake of the <hi type="italic">paronomasia</hi> (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Collectanea</hi>, p. 161). In the conditional clauses the two futures are followed by two preterites (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">Lev 26:21</reference>, which is more in conformity with our western mode of expression), inasmuch as obeying and rebelling are both of them consequences of an act of will: if ye shall be willing, and in consequence of this obey; if ye shall refuse, and rebel against Jehovah. They are therefore, strictly speaking, <hi type="italic">perfecta consecutiva</hi>. According to the ancient mode of writing, the passage <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18-Isa.1.20">Isa 1:18-20</reference> formed a separate <hi type="italic">parashah</hi> by themselves, viz., a <hi type="italic">sethumah</hi>, or <hi type="italic">parashah</hi> indicated by spaces left within the line. The <hi type="italic">piskah</hi> after <reference osisRef="Isa.1.20">Isa 1:20</reference> corresponds to a long pause in the mind of the speaker. - Will Israel tread the saving path of forgiveness thus opened before it, and go on to renewed obedience, and will it be possible for it to be brought back by this path? Individuals possibly may, but not the whole. The divine appeal therefore changes now into a mournful complaint. So peaceful a solution as this of the discord between Jehovah and His children was not to be hoped for. Jerusalem was far too depraved.
entries.9b0257e40fad6f0cabd471e979dcc065702d86d2: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa 1:21</reference> <hi type="italic">“How is she become a harlot, the faithful citadel! she, full of right, lodged in righteousness, and now-murderers.”</hi> It is the keynote of an elegy (<hi type="italic">kinah</hi>) which is sounded here. איכה, and but rarely איך, which is an abbreviated form, is expressive of complaint and amazement. This longer form, like a long-drawn sigh, is a characteristic of the <hi type="italic">kinah</hi>. The <hi type="italic">kinoth</hi> (Lamentations) of Jeremiah commence with it, and receive their title from it; whereas the shorter form is indicative of scornful complaining, and is characteristic of the <hi type="italic">mâshōl</hi> (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.12">Isa 14:12</reference>; Mic 2:4). From this word, which gives the keynote, the rest all follows, soft, full, monotonous, long drawn out and slow, just in the style of an elegy. We may see clearly enough that forms like מלאתי for מלאת, softened by lengthening, were adapted to elegiac compositions, from the first v. of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, where three of these forms occur. Jerusalem had previously been a faithful city, i.e., one stedfastly adhering to the covenant of Jehovah with her (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.78.37">Psa 78:37</reference>).<note placement="foot">We have translated the word <hi type="italic">kiryah</hi> <hi type="italic">“citadel”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Burg</hi>), instead of “city;” but Burg also became the name of the town which sprang up around the citadel, and the persons living in and around the <hi type="italic">Burg</hi> or citadel were called <hi type="italic">burgenses</hi>, “burghers.” Jerusalem, which was also called Zion, might be called, with quite as much right, a citadel (<hi type="italic">Burg</hi>), as a city.</note> <div eID="gen12796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12797" type="x-p"/> This covenant was a marriage covenant. And she had broken it, and had thereby become a <hi type="italic">zonâh</hi> (harlot) - a prophetic view, the germs of which had already been given in the Pentateuch, where the worship of idols on the part of Israel is called whoring after them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">Deu 31:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.15-Exod.34.16">Exo 34:15-16</reference>; in all, seven times). It was not, however, merely gross outward idolatry which made the church of God a “harlot,” but infidelity of heart, in whatever form it might express itself; so that Jesus described the people of His own time as an “adulterous generation,” notwithstanding the pharisaical strictness with which the worship of Jehovah was then observed. For, as the v. before us indicates, this marriage relation was founded upon right and righteousness in the broadest sense: <hi type="italic">mishpat</hi>, <hi type="italic">“right,”</hi> i.e., a realization of right answering to the will of God as positively declared; and <hi type="italic">tzedek</hi>, <hi type="italic">“righteousness,”</hi> i.e., a righteous state moulded by that will, or a righteous course of conduct regulated according to it (somewhat different, therefore, from the more qualitative <hi type="italic">tzedâkâh</hi>). Jerusalem was once full of such right; and righteousness was not merely there in the form of a hastily passing guest, but had come down from above to take up her permanent abode in Jerusalem: she tarried there day and night as if it were her home. The prophet had in his mind the times of David and Solomon, and also more especially the time of Jehoshaphat (about one hundred and fifty years before Isaiah’s appearance), who restored the administration of justice, which had fallen into neglect since the closing years of Solomon’s reign and the time of Rehoboam and Abijah, to which Asa’s reformation had not extended, and re-organized it entirely in the spirit of the law. It is possible also that Jehoiada, the high priest in the time of Joash, may have revived the institutions of Jehoshaphat, so far as they had fallen into disuse under his three godless successors; but even in the second half of the reign of Joash, the administration of justice fell into the same disgraceful state, at least as compared with the times of David, Solomon, and Jehoshaphat, as that in which Isaiah found it. The glaring contrast between the present and the past is indicated by the expression <hi type="italic">“and now.”</hi> In all the correct MSS and editions, <hi type="italic">mishpat</hi> is not accented with <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi>, but with <hi type="italic">rebia</hi>; and <hi type="italic">bâh</hi>, which ought to have <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi>, is accented with <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, on account of the brevity of the following clause. In this way the statement as to the past condition is sufficiently distinguished from that relating to the present.<note placement="foot">It is well known that <hi type="italic">rebia</hi> has less force as a disjunctive than <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, and that <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi> is stronger then either. With regard to the law, according to which <hi type="italic">bâh</hi> has <hi type="italic">rebia</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi>, see Bär, <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 70. To the copies enumerated by Luzzatto, as having the correct accentuation (including Brescia 1494, and Venice, by J. B. Chayim, 1526), we may add Plantin (1582), Buxtorf (1618), Nissel (1662), and many others (cf., Dachselt’s <hi type="italic">Biblia accentuata</hi>, which is not yet out of date).</note> <div eID="gen12797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12798" type="x-p"/> Formerly righteousness, now <hi type="italic">“murderers”</hi> (<hi type="italic">merazzechim</hi>), and indeed, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">rozechim</hi>, murderers by profession, who formed a band, like king Ahab and his son (2Ki 6:32). The contrast was as glaring as possible, since murder is the direct opposite, the most crying violation, of righteousness.
entries.68ebe11865ad918e54cc9a154f9afd43043f4500: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.22">Isa 1:22</reference> <div eID="gen12798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12799" type="x-p"/> The complaint now turns from the city generally to the authorities, and first of all figuratively. <hi type="italic">“Thy silver has become dross, thy drink mutilated with water.”</hi> It is upon this passage that the figurative language of Jer 6:27. and <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.18-Ezek.22.22">Eze 22:18-22</reference> is founded. <hi type="italic">Silver</hi> is here a figurative representation of the princes and lords, with special reference to the nobility of character naturally associated with nobility of birth and rank; for silver - refined silver - is an image of all that is noble and pure, light in all its purity being reflected by it (Bähr, <hi type="italic">Symbolik</hi>, i. 284). The princes and lords had once possessed all the virtues which the Latins called unitedly <hi type="italic">Candor animi</hi>, viz., the virtues of magnanimity, affability, impartiality, and superiority to bribes. This silver had now become <hi type="italic">l'sigim</hi>, dross, or base metal separated (thrown off) from silver in the process of refining (<hi type="italic">sig</hi>, pl. <hi type="italic">sigim</hi>, <hi type="italic">siggim</hi> from <hi type="italic">sug</hi>, <hi type="italic">recedere</hi>, refuse left in smelting, or dross: cf., <reference osisRef="Prov.25.4">Pro 25:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Pro 26:23</reference>). A second figure compares the leading men of the older Jerusalem to good wine, such as drinkers like. The word employed here (<hi type="italic">sobe</hi>) must have been used in this sense by the more cultivated classes in Isaiah’s time (cf., <reference osisRef="Nah.1.10">Nah 1:10</reference>). This pure, strong, and costly wine was now adulterated with water (<hi type="italic">lit. castratum</hi>, according to Pliny’s expression in the <hi type="italic">Natural History:</hi> compare the Horatian phrase, <hi type="italic">jugulare Falernum</hi>), and therefore its strength and odour were weakened, and its worth was diminished. The present was nothing but the dross and shadow of the past. <div eID="gen12799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12800" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.1.23">Isa 1:23</reference> the prophet says this without a figure: <hi type="italic">“Thy rulers are rebellious, and companions of thieves; every one loveth presents, and hunteth after payment; the orphan they right not, and the cause of the widow has no access to them.”</hi> In two words the prophet depicts the contemptible baseness of the national rulers (<hi type="italic">sârim</hi>). He describes first of all their baseness in relation to God, with the alliterative <hi type="italic">sorerim</hi>: <hi type="italic">rebellious</hi>, refractory; and then, in relation to men, <hi type="italic">companions</hi> of thieves, inasmuch as they allowed themselves to be bribed by presents of stolen goods to acts of injustice towards those who had been robbed. They not only willingly accepted such bribes, and that not merely a few of them, but every individual belonging to the rank of princes (<hi type="italic">Cullo</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">haccol</hi>, the whole: every one <hi type="italic">loveth</hi> gifts); but they went eagerly in pursuit of them (<hi type="italic">rodeph</hi>). It was not peace (<hi type="italic">shâlom</hi>) that they hunted after (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">Psa 34:16</reference>), but <hi type="italic">shalmonim</hi>shalmonim, things that would pacify their avarice; not what was good, but compensation for their partiality. - This was the existing state of Jerusalem, and therefore it would hardly be likely to take the way of mercy opened before it in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference>; consequently Jehovah would avail himself of other means of setting it right.
entries.b7bf9714cf5d16e37493e67ef7204bb9a39295c1: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa 1:24</reference> <hi type="italic">“Therefore, saying of the Lord, of Jehovah of hosts, of the Strong One of Israel: Ah! I will relieve myself on mine adversaries, and will avenge myself upon mine enemies.”</hi> Salvation through judgment was the only means of improvement and preservation left to the congregation, which called itself by the name of Jerusalem. Jehovah would therefore afford satisfaction to His holiness, and administer a judicial sifting to Jerusalem. There is no other passage in Isaiah in which we meet with such a crowding together of different names of God as we do here (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Isa 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">Isa 10:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>). With three names, descriptive of the irresistible omnipotence of God, the irrevocable decree of a sifting judgment is sealed. The word נאּם, which is used here instead of אמר and points back to a verb נאם, related to נהם and המה, corresponds to the deep, earnest pathos of the words. These verbs, which are imitations of sounds, all denote a dull hollow groaning. The word used here, therefore, signifies that which is spoken with significant secrecy and solemn softness. It is never written absolutely, but is always followed by the subject who speaks (saying of Jehovah it is, i.e., Jehovah says). We meet with it first of all in Gen 22:16. In the prophetic writings it occurs in Obadiah and Joel, but most frequently in Jeremiah and Ezekiel. It is generally written at the close of the sentence, or parenthetically in the middle; very rarely at the commencement, as it is here and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1Sa 2:30</reference> and Psa 110:1. The “saying” commences with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (<hi type="italic">ah!</hi>), the painfulness of pity being mingled with the determined outbreak of wrath. By the side of the niphal <hi type="italic">nikkam min</hi> (to be revenged upon a person) we find the niphal <hi type="italic">nicham</hi> (lit. to console one’s self). The two words are derived from kindred roots. The latter is conjugated with <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi> in the preformative syllable, the former with <hi type="italic">i</hi>, according to the older system of vowel-pointing adopted in the East.<note placement="foot">The so-called Assyrian mode of pointing, which was entirely supplanted, with the exception of a few relics, by the Tiberian mode which now lies before us, has no <hi type="italic">seghol</hi> (see <hi type="italic">DMZ</hi>. xviii. 322). According to Luzzatto (<hi type="italic">Proleg</hi>. p. 200), they wrote <hi type="italic">ektol</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">iktol</hi>, to avoid confounding it with יקטל, which was pronounced <hi type="italic">iktol</hi>, and not <hi type="italic">yiktol</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12801" type="x-p"/> Jehovah would procure Himself relief from His enemies by letting out upon them the wrath with which He had hitherto been burdened (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Eze 5:13</reference>). He now calls the masses of Jerusalem by their right name. <div eID="gen12801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12802" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference> states clearly in what the revenge consisted with which Jehovah was inwardly burdened (<hi type="italic">innakmah</hi>, a cohortative with the <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, indicating internal oppression): <hi type="italic">“And I will bring my hand over thee, and will smelt out thy dross as with alkali, and will clear away all thy lead.”</hi> As long as God leaves a person’s actions or sufferings alone, His hand, i.e., His acting, is at rest. Bringing the hand over a person signifies a movement of the hand, which has been hitherto at rest, either for the purpose of inflicting judicial punishment upon the person named (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.8">Amo 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.9">Jer 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.12">Eze 38:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.81.15">Psa 81:15</reference>), or else, though this is seldom the case, for the purpose of saving him (Zec 13:7). The reference here is to the divine treatment of Jerusalem, in which punishment and salvation were combined - punishment as the means, salvation as the end. The interposition of Jehovah was, as it were, a smelting, which would sweep away, not indeed Jerusalem itself, but the ungodly in Jerusalem. They are compared to dross, or (as the verb seems to imply) to ore mixed with dross, and, inasmuch as lead is thrown off in the smelting of silver, to such ingredients of lead as Jehovah would speedily and thoroughly remove, <hi type="italic">“like alkali,”</hi> i.e., “as if with alkali” (<hi type="italic">Cabbo</hi>r, <hi type="italic">Comparatio decurtata</hi>, for <hi type="italic">C'babbor</hi>: for this mode of dropping <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> after <hi type="italic">Caph</hi>, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.22.13">Lev 22:13</reference>, and many other passages). By <hi type="italic">bedilim</hi> (from <hi type="italic">bâdal</hi>, to separate) we are to understand the several pieces of <hi type="italic">stannum</hi> or lead<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Plumbum nigrum</hi>, says Pliny, <hi type="italic">n. n.</hi> xxiv. 16, is sometimes found alone, and sometimes mixed with silver: <hi type="italic">ejus qui primus fluic in fornacibus liquor, stannum appellatur</hi>. The reference here is to the lead separated from the ore in the process of obtaining pure silver. In the form of powder this dross is called <hi type="italic">bedil</hi>, and the pieces <hi type="italic">bedilim</hi>; whereas <hi type="italic">ophereth</hi> is the name of solid lead, obtained by simply melting down from ore which does not contain silver. The fact that <hi type="italic">bedil</hi> is also apparently used as a name for tin, may be explained in the same way as the homonymy of iron and basalt (<hi type="italic">Com. on </hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.2">Job 28:2</reference>), and of the oak and terebinth. The two metals are called by the same name on account of their having a certain outward resemblance, viz., in softness, pliability, colour, and specific gravity.</note> in which the silver is contained, and which are separated by smelting, all the baser metals being distinguished from the purer kinds by the fact that they are combustible (i.e., can be oxidized). Both <hi type="italic">bor</hi>, or potash (an alkali obtained from land-plants), and <hi type="italic">nether</hi>, natron (i.e., soda, or natron obtained from the ashes of marine plants, which is also met with in many mineral waters), have been employed from the very earliest times to accelerate the process of smelting, for the purpose of separating a metal from its ore.
entries.6cc7c0cf4d5e0cb56bae16cb385bba6382a5ce52: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference> <div eID="gen12802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12803" type="x-p"/> As the threat couched in the previous figure does not point to the destruction, but simply to the smelting of Jerusalem, there is nothing strange in the fact that in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa 1:26</reference> it should pass over into a pure promise; the meltingly soft and yearningly mournful termination of the clauses with <hi type="italic">ayich</hi>, the keynote of the later songs of Zion, being still continued. <hi type="italic">“And I will bring back thy judges as in the olden time, and thy counsellors as in the beginning; afterwards thou wilt be called city of righteousness, faithful citadel.”</hi> The threat itself was, indeed, relatively a promise, inasmuch as whatever could stand the fire would survive the judgment; and the distinct object of this was to bring back Jerusalem to the purer metal of its own true nature. But when that had been accomplished, still more would follow. The indestructible kernel that remained would be crystallized, since Jerusalem would receive back from Jehovah the judges and counsellors which it had had in the olden flourishing times of the monarchy, ever since it had become the city of David and of the temple; not, indeed, the very same persons, but persons quite equal to them in excellence. Under such God-given leaders Jerusalem would become what it had once been, and what it ought to be. The names applied to the city indicate the impression produced by the manifestation of its true nature. The second name is written without the article, as in fact the word <hi type="italic">kiryah</hi> (city), with its massive, definite sound, always is in Isaiah. Thus did Jehovah announce the way which it had been irrevocably determined that He would take with Israel, as the only way to salvation. Moreover, this was the fundamental principle of the government of God, the law of Israel’s history. <div eID="gen12803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12804" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.27">Isa 1:27</reference> presents it in a brief and concise form: <hi type="italic">“Sion will be redeemed through judgment, and her returning ones through righteousness.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Mishpat</hi> and <hi type="italic">tzedâkâh</hi> are used elsewhere for divine gifts (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>), for such conduct as is pleasing to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.16">Isa 32:16</reference>), and for royal Messianic virtues (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3-Isa.11.5">Isa 11:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Isa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">Isa 32:1</reference>). Here, however, where we are helped by the context, they are to be interpreted according to such parallel passages as <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">Isa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.16">Isa 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa 28:17</reference>, as signifying God’s right and righteousness in their primarily judicious self-fulfilment. A judgment, on the part of God the righteous One, would be the means by which Zion itself, so far as it had remained faithful to Jehovah, and those who were converted in the midst of the judgment, would be redeemed - a judgment upon sinners and sin, by which the power that had held in bondage the divine nature of Zion, so far as it still continued to exist, would be broken, and in consequence of which those who turned to Jehovah would be incorporated into His true church. Whilst, therefore, God was revealing Himself in His punitive righteousness; He was working out a righteousness which would be bestowed as a gift of grace upon those who escaped the former. The notion of “righteousness” is now following a New Testament track. In front it has the fire of the law; behind, the love of the gospel. Love is concealed behind the wrath, like the sun behind the thunder-clouds. Zion, so far as it truly is or is becoming Zion, is redeemed, and none but the ungodly are destroyed. But, as is added in the next verse, the latter takes place without mercy.
entries.52fcbd8d7f05d74ec4093fdb6f9b4c6255c5638f: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.28">Isa 1:28</reference> <hi type="italic">“And breaking up of the rebellious and sinners together; and those who forsake Jehovah will perish.”</hi> The judicial side of the approaching act of redemption is here expressed in a way that all can understand. The exclamatory substantive clause in the first half of the v. is explained by a declaratory verbal clause in the second. The <hi type="italic">“rebellious”</hi> were those who had both inwardly and outwardly broken away from Jehovah; <hi type="italic">“sinners,”</hi> those who were living in open sins; and <hi type="italic">“those who forsake Jehovah,”</hi> such as had become estranged from God in either of these ways. <div eID="gen12804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12805" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference> declares how God’s judgment of destruction would fall upon all of these. The v. is introduced with an explanatory “for” (<hi type="italic">Chi</hi>): <hi type="italic">“For they become ashamed of the terebinths, in which ye had your delight; and ye must blush for the gardens, in which ye took pleasure.”</hi> The terebinths and gardens (the second word with the article, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8">Hab 3:8</reference>, first <hi type="italic">binharim</hi>, then <hi type="italic">banneharim</hi>) are not referred to as objects of luxury, as Hitzig and Drechsler assume, but as unlawful places of worship and objects of worship (see <reference osisRef="Deut.16.21">Deu 16:21</reference>). They are both of them frequently mentioned by the prophets in this sense (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.5">Isa 57:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.3">Isa 65:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.17">Isa 66:17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Châmor</hi> and <hi type="italic">bâchar</hi> are also the words commonly applied to an arbitrary choice of false gods (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.24">Isa 41:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>), and <hi type="italic">bosh min</hi> is the general phrase used to denote the shame which falls upon idolaters, when the worthlessness of their idols becomes conspicuous through their impotence. On the difference between <hi type="italic">bosh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Châpher</hi>, see the comm. on Psa 35:4.<note placement="foot">It is perfectly certain that <hi type="italic">Châpher</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">Chaphira</hi>, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">Châphar</hi>, <hi type="italic">hafara</hi>, to dig) signifies to blush, <hi type="italic">erubescere</hi>; but the combination of <hi type="italic">bosh</hi> and <hi type="italic">yâbash</hi> (<hi type="italic">bâda</hi>), which would give <hi type="italic">albescere</hi> or <hi type="italic">expallescere</hi> (to turn white or pale) as the primary idea of <hi type="italic">bosh</hi>, has not only the Arabic use of <hi type="italic">bayyada</hi> and <hi type="italic">ibyadda</hi> (to rejoice, be made glad) against it, but above all the dialectic <hi type="italic">bechath</hi>, <hi type="italic">bahita</hi> (<hi type="italic">bahuta</hi>), which, when taken in connection with <hi type="italic">bethath</hi> (<hi type="italic">batta</hi>), points rather to the primary idea of being cut off (<hi type="italic">abscindi</hi>: cf., <hi type="italic">spes abscissa</hi>). See Lane’s <hi type="italic">Arabic-English Lexicon</hi>, i. 263.</note> <div eID="gen12805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12806" type="x-p"/> The word <hi type="italic">elim</hi> is erroneously translated “idols” in the Septuagint and other ancient versions. The feeling which led to this, however, was a correct one, since the places of worship really stand for the idols worshipped in those places.<note placement="foot">With regard to the derivation, <hi type="italic">êlim</hi>, whether used in the sense of strong men, or gods, or rams, or terebinths, is still but one word, derived from <hi type="italic">ı̄l</hi> or <hi type="italic">ūl</hi>, so that in all three senses it may be written either with or without <hi type="italic">Yod</hi>. Nevertheless <hi type="italic">elim</hi> in the sense of “rams” only occurs without <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> in Job 42:8. In the sense of “gods” it is always written without <hi type="italic">Yod</hi>; in that of “strong men” with <hi type="italic">Yod</hi>. In the singular the name of the terebinth is always written <hi type="italic">elah</hi> without <hi type="italic">Yod</hi>; in the plural, however, it is written either with or without. But this no more presupposes a singular <hi type="italic">êl</hi> (<hi type="italic">ayil</hi>) in common use, than <hi type="italic">bêtzim</hi> presupposes a singular <hi type="italic">bêts</hi> (<hi type="italic">bayits</hi>); still the word <hi type="italic">êl</hi> with <hi type="italic">Yod</hi> does occur once, viz., in Gen 14:6. <hi type="italic">Allâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">allōn</hi>, an oak, also spring from the same root, namely <hi type="italic">âlal</hi> = <hi type="italic">il</hi>; just as in Arabic both <hi type="italic">ı̄l</hi> and <hi type="italic">ill</hi> are used for <hi type="italic">ēl</hi> (God); and <hi type="italic">âl</hi> and <hi type="italic">ill</hi>, in the sense of relationship, point to a similar change in the form of the root.</note> <div eID="gen12806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12807" type="x-p"/> The excited state of the prophet at the close of his prophecy is evinced by his abrupt leap from an exclamation to a direct address (Ges. §137, Anm. 3).
entries.ac9a07918ec1cf3cb200bf740af9f217e58071c7: <reference osisRef="Isa.1.30">Isa 1:30</reference> <div eID="gen12807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12808" type="x-p"/> He still continues in the same excitement, piling a second explanatory sentence upon the first, and commencing this also with <hi type="italic">“for”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Chi</hi>); and then, carried away by the association of ideas, he takes terebinths and gardens as the future figures of the idolatrous people themselves.  <hi type="italic">“For ye shall become like a terebinth with withered leaves, and like a garden that hath no water.” </hi> Their prosperity is distroyed, so that they resemble a terebinth withered as to its leaves, which in other cases are always green (<hi type="italic">nobleth ‛aleah</hi>, genitives connection according to (Ges. §112, 2). Their sources of help are dried up, so that they are like a garden without water, and therefore waste. In this withered state terebinths and gardens, to which the idolatrous are compared, are easily set on fire. All that is wanted is a spark to kindle them, when they are immediately in flames. <hi type="italic"></hi> <div eID="gen12808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12809" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.31">Isa 1:31</reference> shows in a third figure where this spark was to come from: <hi type="italic">“And the rich man becomes tow, and his work the spark; and they will both burn together, and no one extinguishes them.”</hi> The form <hi type="italic">poalo</hi> suggests at first a participial meaning (its maker), but החסון would be a very unusual epithet to apply to an idol. Moreover, the figure itself would be a distorted one, since the natural order would be, that the idol would be the thing that kindled the fire, and the man the object to be set on fire, and not the reverse. We therefore follow the lxx, Targ., and Vulg., with Gesenius and other more recent grammarians, and adopt the rendering “his work” (<hi type="italic">opus ejus</hi>). The forms פּעלו and פּעלו (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa 52:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jer 22:13</reference>) are two equally admissible changes of the ground-form פעלו (פּעלו). As <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference> refers to idolatrous worship, <hi type="italic">poalo</hi> (his work) is an idol, a god made by human hands (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.19">Isa 37:19</reference>, etc.). The prosperous idolater, who could give gold and silver for idolatrous images out of the abundance of his possessions (<hi type="italic">Châson</hi> is to be interpreted in accordance with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">Isa 33:6</reference>), becomes <hi type="italic">tow</hi> (talm. “the refuse of flax:” the radical meaning is to shake out, viz., in combing), and the idol the <hi type="italic">spark</hi> which sets this mass of fibre in flames, so that they are both irretrievably consumed. For the fire of judgment, by which sinners are devoured, need not come from without. Sin carries the fire of indignation within itself. And an idol is, as it were, an idolater’s sin embodied and exposed to the light of day. <div eID="gen12809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12810" type="x-p"/> The date of the composition of this first prophecy is a puzzle. Caspari thoroughly investigated every imaginary possibility, and at last adopted the conclusion that it dates from the time of Uzziah, inasmuch as <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:7-9</reference> do not relate to an actual, but merely to an ideal, present. But notwithstanding all the acuteness with which Caspari has worked out his view, it still remains a very forced one. The oftener we return to the reading of this prophetic address, the stronger is our impression that <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:7-9</reference> contain a description of the state of things which really existed at the time when the words were spoken. There were actually two devastations of the land of Judah which occurred during the ministry of Isaiah, and in which Jerusalem was only spared by the miraculous interposition of Jehovah: one under Ahaz in the year of the Syro-Ephraimitish war; the other under Hezekiah, when the Assyrian forces laid the land waste but were scattered at last in their attack upon Jerusalem. The year of the Syro-Ephraimitish war is supported by Gesenius, Rosenmüller (who expresses a different opinion in every one of the three editions of his <hi type="italic">Scholia</hi>), Maurer, Movers, Knobel, Hävernick, and others; the time of the Assyrian oppression by Hitzig, Umbreit, Drechsler, and Luzzatto. Now, whichever of these views we may adopt, there will still remain, as a test of its admissiblity, the difficult question, How did this prophecy come to stand at the head of the book, if it belonged to the time of Uzziah-Jotham? This question, upon which the solution of the difficulty depends, can only be settled when we come to <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Isa 6:1</reference>-13. Till then, the date of the composition of chapter 1 must be left undecided. It is enough for the present to know, that, according to the accounts given in the books of Kings and Chronicles, there were two occasions when the situation of Jerusalem resembled the one described in the present chapter.  <chapter eID="Isa.1"/> <div eID="gen12810" type="x-p"/>

entries.ada3bb22d5f91b5a95403639b96bbf4563c37132: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.1.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.1.1" sID="gen40308" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">The vision of Isaiah</hi> The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">חזון</foreign> (<hi type="italic">chazon</hi>,) though it is derived from <foreign xml:lang="he">חזה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">chazah</hi>,) <hi type="italic">he saw</hi>, and literally is <hi type="italic">a vision</hi>, yet commonly signifies <hi type="italic">a prophecy</hi>. For when the Scripture makes mention of special visions which were exhibited to the prophets in a symbolical manner, when it was the will of God that some extraordinary event should receive confirmation, in such cases the word Tibet, (<foreign xml:lang="he">מראה</foreign>,) <hi type="italic">vision</hi>, is employed. Not to multiply quotations, in a passage which relates <hi type="italic">to prophecy</hi> in general the writer says, that <hi type="italic">the word of God was precious, because</hi> <foreign xml:lang="he">חזון</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">chazon</hi>,) <hi type="italic">vision, was of rare occurrence</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.3.1">1 Samuel 3:1</reference>.) A little afterwards, the word <foreign xml:lang="he">מראה</foreign>: (mar-ah) is employed to denote the vision by which God revealed himself to Samuel. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.3.13">1 Samuel 3:13</reference>.) In distinguishing between two ordinary methods of revelation, <hi type="italic">a vision and a dream</hi>, Moses speaks of <hi type="italic">a vision</hi> (<foreign xml:lang="he">מראה</foreign>) as the special method. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Num.12.6">Numbers 12:6</reference>.) It is evident, however, that <hi type="italic">the seer</hi>, <foreign xml:lang="he">הראה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">haroeh</hi>,) was the name formerly given to prophets, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.9">1 Samuel 9:9</reference>;) but by way of excellence, because God revealed to them his counsel in a familiar manner.<div eID="gen40309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40310" type="x-p"/>So far as relates to the present passage, this word unquestionably denotes the certainty of the doctrine; as if it had been said that there is nothing contained in this book which was not made known to <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> by God himself. The derivation of the word, therefore, deserves attention; for we learn by it that the prophets did not speak of their own accord, or draw from their own imaginations, but that they were enlightened by God, who opened their eyes to perceive those things which otherwise they would not of themselves have been able to comprehend. Thus the inscription of Isaiah recommends to us the doctrine of this book, as containing no human reasonings, but the oracles of God, in order to convince us that it contains nothing but what was revealed by the Spirit of God.<div eID="gen40310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40311" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Concerning Judah</hi> Were we to render it to <hi type="italic">Judah</hi>, it would make little difference, for the preposition <foreign xml:lang="he">על</foreign> (<hi type="italic">al</hi>) has both significations, and the meaning will still be, that everything contained in this book belongs strictly to <hi type="italic">Judah and Jerusalem.</hi> For though many things are scattered through it which relate to Babylon, Egypt, Tyre, and other cities and countries, yet it was not necessary that those places should be expressly enumerated in the title; for nothing more was required than to announce the principal subject, and to explain to whom Isaiah was chiefly sent, that is, <hi type="italic">to Jerusalem, and the Jews</hi>. Everything else that is contained in his prophecies may be said to have been accidental and foreign to the subject.<div eID="gen40311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40312" type="x-p"/>And yet it was not inconsistent with his office to make known to other nations the calamities which should overtake them; for in like manner Amos did not go beyond the limits of his calling, when he did not spare the Jews, though he was not sent to them. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Amos.2.4 Bible:Amos.2.5">Amos 2:4, 5</reference>.) A still more familiar instance is found in the calling of Peter and Paul, the former of whom was appointed to the Jews, and the latter to the Gentiles. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.8">Galatians 2:8</reference>.) And yet Peter did not rush beyond the limits of his office, by preaching to the Gentiles; as, for example, when he went to Cornelius: (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.17">Acts 10:17</reference>:) nor did Paul, when he offered his services to the Jews, to whom he immediately went as soon as he entered into any city. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.5 Bible:Acts.14.1 Bible:Acts.17.2 Bible:Acts.17.10 Bible:Acts.18.4 Bible:Acts.18.19">Acts 13:5; 14:1; 17:2, 10; 18:4,19</reference>.) In the same light ought we to view Isaiah; for while he is careful to instruct the Jews, and directs his labors expressly towards that object, he does not transgress his proper limits when he likewise takes a passing notice of other nations.<div eID="gen40312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40313" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Judah and Jerusalem</hi> He takes <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> for the whole nation, and <hi type="italic">Jerusalem</hi> for the chief city in the kingdom; for he does not make a distinction between <hi type="italic">Jerusalem</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Jews</hi>, but mentions it, by way of eminence, (<foreign xml:lang="el">κατ ᾿ ἐξοχὴν,</foreign>) as the metropolis, just as if a prophet of the present day were to address the kingdom of France, and Paris, which is the metropolis of the nation. And this was of great importance, that the inhabitants of Jerusalem might not hold themselves exempted, as if they were free from all blame, or placed above the laws on account of their high rank, and thus might send the meaner sort of people to be instructed by homely prophets. It is a mistake, however, to suppose that <hi type="italic">Jerusalem </hi>is mentioned separately, on account of its being situated in the tribe of Benjamin; for the half of that tribes which was subject to the posterity of David, is included under the name of <hi type="italic">Judah</hi><div eID="gen40313" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.1.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen40308" osisID="Isa.1.1" type="section"/>
entries.e0fe250a768a042db444abcf93a0547717cd9623:
2. Hear, O heavens Isaiah has here imitated Moses, as all the prophets are accustomed to do; and there cannot be a doubt that he alludes to that illustrious Song of Moses, in which, at the very commencement, he calls heaven and earth to witness against the people:
Give ear, O ye heavens, and I will speak; and hear, O earth, the words of my mouth. (Deuteronomy 32:1.)
This is unquestionably a very severe protestation; for it conveys this meaning, that both turn to the elements which are dumb and devoid of feeling, because men have now no ears, or are bereft of all their senses. The Prophet, therefore, speaks of it as an extraordinary and monstrous thing, which ought to strike even the senseless elements with amazement. For what could be more shocking than that the Israelites should revolt from God, who had bestowed on them so many benefits? Those who think that by heaven are meant angels, and by earth men, weaken too much the import of those words, and thus destroy all their force and majesty.
Almost all the commentators consider the clause to end with the words, for the Lord hath spoken; as if the Prophet had intimated, that as soon as the Lord opens his sacred mouth, all ought to be attentive to hear his voice.
